en: Preface to the Record of the Brahmajāla Sūtra:
The "Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Precepts Chapter" of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* spoken by the Tathāgata was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Western Heavens under imperial decree;
it constitutes one chapter within the original extensive version. Its presence in the Great Canon [is] with the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*...
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* (contained within the volume beginning with the character "Tóng"), it is stated that those who uphold this sutra possess five kinds of merit:
either the Buddhas of the ten directions take pity on them and constantly protect them; or at the time of death, they possess right view and their minds are filled with joy;

or in every place of rebirth, they have pure bodhisattvas as companions; or they fully accomplish the accumulation of merit and the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); or in future lives, their nature [is transformed].
When morality, merit, and wisdom are perfected, this is the sphere of the Buddha’s activity; let the wise contemplate and examine this well.
Alas! Because of the Tathāgata’s great vows, his supernatural powers, and his compassion for sentient beings, he is sincere, truthful, and not false.
The Dharma Master Aoyu of Sekibaku believed this most deeply; thereupon, he composed this explanatory record, inviting from afar the Japanese master Gyunyo Shōkō to follow him.
This manuscript was obtained from the Great Song Kingdom and presented to me; I rejoiced in it with admiration and immediately transcribed it at the Zen Hall of Mount Fuku-san in Kamo.
May all fellow practitioners, both monastics and laypeople who share this aspiration, find joy in it. I pray that those who see, hear, or rejoice in this shall plant the seeds of contentment;
through recitation and contemplation, may they realize the Dharma-seal of the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya), awaken one another, and together be liberated from the depths of saṃsāra.
Rin. Recorded by the śramaṇa Kōben of the Zen-dō-in at Mount Hōko,
Kamogawa, during the latter part of the eleventh month in the third year of the Shōkū era.
Record of the Brahmajāla Sūtra, Volume One (Preface), composed by the Śramaṇa Chuǎn’ào of Shíbì Temple in Beijing.
The *Prātimokṣa* is the teacher of Bodhisattvas; even the slightest virtue must be recorded, and even the most minute flaw must be punished.

Withdrawing to guard the subtle and profound, and advancing to prevent unwholesome speech and action, it serves as the stairway to the ten thousand virtues and the fountainhead of the ten bodies [of the Buddha].

Thus, it is only fitting that the Lotus Treasury (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka) was personally proclaimed by the Buddha, and the Thousand-Flower Sūtra (Sahasrapuṣpa-sūtra) was subsequently received by his disciples as the essential points for study.
Yet, since its initial emergence under the Yao Qin dynasty, it has passed through distant ages; its branches have spread throughout the world, and those who chant and recite it are truly numerous.

Regarding its essential meaning, there are few who truly understand it; although the commentaries composed by the masters of old are extensive and their exegesis rich, later disciples merely contemplate them without putting them into practice.
Although the monks here in this land mostly study the Mahāyāna, though they receive the provisional name of *śrāvaka*, their conduct is that of a Bodhisattva.
To have few faults and little regret, one must truly possess deep understanding; without such an elucidation, it will ultimately be difficult to establish [the teaching).

Because this work is a separate circulation of the *Guang shu* (Extensive Commentary), there are points where it differs; I have thus made considerable revisions and ventured to set forth my own humble views to connect with the entire text.
If its subtle essence can be attained, then the trap and snare may be said to have served their purpose.
I take refuge in the Buddhas of the three periods of time, In the full-worded Sūtras, And in the Bodhisattva Saṅgha of the ten directions;
may you grant your compassionate protection. I now briefly praise and describe the Prātimokṣa, Which universally benefits all sentient beings And causes them to turn toward the path of Bodhi.
This commentary on the Bodhisattva Precept Sūtra is divided into two main parts:
first, an explanation of the title—*The Brahmajāla Sūtra Spoken by Vairocana Buddha, Chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, the Bodhisattva Precept Text*.
The commentary explains that this is divided into two parts. The first three characters constitute the general title of the section;

"Brahmajāla" (梵網) is the metaphor. "Brahma" refers to Brahmā; in full, it is *Brahmāloka*, which means "Utmost Purity. Because he is free from desire and defilement, he receives the name "Utmost Pure.
"Jāla" (網) refers to the banner-net of that heaven; because he holds this [sūtra] and proceeds to the assembly of the Buddhas, it is so named.
Regarding the middle offering: when the Buddha saw [the assembly] listening to the Dharma, he took this as an analogy. There are both general and specific analogies;

the "general" refers to the differences in the dispositions and capacities of sentient beings, for the Buddhist teachings bestowed upon them likewise differ accordingly. Thus, the subsequent text says:
"Seated at the site of the tranquil extinction (śānta-mārga-maṇḍala) upon the Vajra-flower-light-king throne, [extending] even to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara."

In the context of the successive ten stages (*bhūmi*) as explained therein, when the Buddha observed the Great Brahma Kings Net-Canopy Banner (*Jāla-dhvaja*), he spoke for their sake of how immeasurable worlds are like the mesh of a net;

each and every world is distinct and different from one another, and the gateways to the immeasurable Buddha-teachings are likewise so. This distinction refers to the Bodhisattva’s threefold purity (*tri-koṭi-pariśuddhi*).
First, the precept of restraining one's conduct (*saṃvara-śīla*) is like a net spread over trees; birds and vermin cannot invade it.

Second, the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) is like a tree that, having obtained a net, produces flowers and fruit in abundance; these two support one another.

Third, the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*) is like casting a net into a river so that fish emerge onto the bank. Furthermore, according to what is explained in the following text, the Buddha—
From beneath the Bodhi tree up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the ten assemblies of the Dharma-gate are taught;
the first nine constitute that which is taught by the general discourse (*sāmānya-nirdeśa*), while the tenth constitutes that which is taught by the specific discourse (*viśeṣa-nirdeśa*).

Furthermore, the general necessarily encompasses the specific, whereas the specific does not encompass the general. The "Sūtra" refers to that which is taught by one portion of the discourse; its meanings are manifold.
The general principle of the section’s structure is as previously discussed. The two instances of "Vairocana" below constitute the specific headings for this chapter.
Within these, there are both general and specific aspects; the general refers to the overall title of the chapter, while the specific refers to the distinct meanings within the chapter.
First, Vairocana Buddha is the primary speaker. "Vairocana" is translated here as "Fullness" (Pūrṇa).
Because all defilements and obstacles—whether coarse or subtle—are purified without exception, a Buddha (the Sanskrit term *buddha* is fully rendered as *buddha*;
this is translated here as "the Awakened One") is one whose awakening is perfectly pure. "Awakening" (*bodhi*) refers to the person;

it distinguishes [the Buddha] from other vehicles and bodhisattvas, who possess only partial or incomplete awakening. Thus, retaining the abbreviated form from the Sanskrit, we simply call him a "Buddha."

However, according to the Sanskrit original, it is called Vairocana, which here means "Universal Illumination" (*Guāngmíng Biànzhào*), because the two lights of body and wisdom illuminate both internally and externally.

While the former [explanation] refers to the departure from obstacles and this one refers to the manifestation of virtues—though these two approaches differ in their paths, they converge on the same principle—the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" consists of sixty-one chapters; this [section] selects [from among them].
It is not others; "mind" refers to the mind that is cultivated and brought forth, namely the fifty minds beginning with faith.

"Ground" (bhūmi) refers to the stages upon which one relies and which are accomplished, namely the three grounds. The stage prior to these grounds is collectively named the Ground of Faithful Practice (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*);

the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) is named the Ground of Pure Mind (*vimalā-bhūmi*); and the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) and above are collectively named the Ground of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*). These grounds have their respective births.
It is explained by means of this because it fulfills the meaning of "bearing" (*dhāraṇa*); for within these three stages, one can produce and bear all meritorious qualities.

Since there is nothing that is not a sublime practice, and it is called a "gate" (*mukha*) because it is a path through which the noble ones (*ārya*) universally travel, it is designated as a "chapter" (*varga*) because the categories differ.
As for the "Bodhisattva Precept Text" (*Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*), it refers to the specific meaning contained within this chapter; thus it is so named.
Furthermore, because there are other doctrinal meanings, it is not so [as previously stated]. In the following section, why is it necessary to separately designate the meaning of "Bodhisattva"?

It is as explained in the standard interpretation: "Precept" (*śīla*) carries the meaning of filial obedience and the meaning of restraint. To explain extensively below, "the root" refers to the source of the Bodhisattva;
thus, "precept" is the root, which is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. "The precept of the Bodhisattva" is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound based on the root.
This is the explanation. If one discusses this in terms of the fruit [of Buddhahood], it is also the fundamental basis of the Buddha;

therefore, the subsequent text states: "The source of all Buddhas, the root of practicing the bodhisattva path. Now, for the sake of those who are the primary audience, we speak only of the bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, since the two categories of light and heavy precepts do not exhaust the full range of monastic rules, they are spoken of in brief; this brevity serves as the foundation for the detailed exposition that follows in each section.

All these refer to extensive texts such as the eighty thousand *vyañjana* (syllables) in the *Vinaya-vastu* and other sections. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Briefly, there are eighty thousand [dharmas];
extensively, they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. One should know that what is presented here is the most concise of the concise. As it is said below: "It is like the tip of a hair;
yet one who knows the spring and autumn of heaven and earth can discern this from a single leaf. When the perfect pivot is confronted with this, it is sufficient to infer the three remaining sides.

In this title, there are two layers of general and specific designations, which can be understood by examining them in detail. Thus, both Dharma and analogy are manifested, and both the Master’s teaching and the instruction are presented together;

the expressed meaning is established in its entirety, and both the general and the specific are given their names. Because the phrasing is concise yet the principles are exhaustive, it is placed at the beginning of the work;
hence it is called the *Brahmajāla*, etc. However, regarding the broad discussion of the Bodhisattva precepts, according to the tradition passed down from Master Kumārajīva:
In the Western Regions, there exists a work of one hundred thousand stanzas in sixty-one chapters; if translated in its entirety, it would comprise more than three hundred fascicles.

Because Master Kumārajīva upheld the Bodhisattva precepts, he devoted himself single-mindedly to reciting the "Chapter on the Ground of the Mind" (*Cittabhūmi-dharmamukha*), which briefly elucidates the characteristics of the Bodhisattva precepts.
When he arrived in this land, it was during the reign of Yao Xing, and he translated and transmitted over fifty treatises and sūtras.
Finally, when this sūtra was translated within the Xiaoyao Garden in the third year of the Hongshi era, the remaining extensive sections had not yet reached this region;
thus, the explanation of the title is hereby completed.

From here below begins the second part, the explanation of the main text. The main text has three sections: first, the section on the source from which the precepts arise; second, the section on the formal exposition based on conditions;

and third, the section on the concluding exhortation for circulation. Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, the prose (long passage), and second, the verse (repeated stanza). Within the first of these, there are two parts:

first, the general indication of the root and the branches, as well as the extensive and the concise; and second, the specific clarification of the origins and lineages of the True and the Emanated. Within the first of these, there are two parts.
First, the explicit explanation:

At that time, Vairocana Buddha, for the sake of this great assembly, briefly opened up from among the dharma-gates of the hundred thousand Ganges-sands of ineffable teachings a portion of the Ground of the Mind (cittabhūmi) no larger than a hair-tip.

The commentary states: "At that time" means "at that very moment," specifically the time when Vairocana was transmitting [the teaching] to Śākyamuni within the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*).
Vairocana Buddha is the principal speaker; his true nature is as briefly described previously.
"For this great assembly" refers to those prior to the stages (the three levels of the *prthagjana* and the ten stages of the *bodhisattva*) and all ordinary beings.
"Briefly opening" refers to the Dharma that is being expounded; "briefly" means concisely. Regarding the matter of the Ganges, it is explained in the same way as in other passages.
"Inexpressible" (anabhilāpya) refers to what is stated in the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra: the intention of the "great number" is to clarify that one grain of sand constitutes one "inexpressible.
Thus, there are hundreds of thousands of grains of sand from the Ganges, up to an "inexpressible" number; this serves as the countable object.
Regarding these numerical dharma-gates, the dharmas that are enumerated consist precisely of this many dharma-gates; all of them were taught by Śākyamuni.

As for the phrase "the mind-ground being only the size of a hair-tip," it means that from among the vast and manifold dharmas, only a small portion is briefly explained—likened to a hair-tip—for the sake of the assembly prior to the bhūmis. [The interlocutor] asks: Why are they not explained in their entirety? Now...
To explain briefly: even those at the stage of Good Intelligence (Sādhumati) cannot yet receive the Dharma like rain from the clouds;
how much less could a vessel the size of a *doudie* (a small measure) possess the capacity of the great ocean? Therefore, it is impossible.

This is stated by looking back from the fundamental to the derivative, pointing forward to the stages prior to the Grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), meaning that Vairocana personally bestowed [the teaching] upon that assembly, and that assembly consists of the emanations of Śākyamuni.
Because it was bestowed by the Father [the Buddha], this refers to the time when the Master convenes the assembly; only then does one know it to be the time of the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*).

It is only by taking the Dharma to gather the multitude that one knows these to be the assembly prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*). This is merely Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s introductory arrangement here;
the same applies to the subsequent passages. This is the great opening of the Dharma-gate to reveal a small portion of the Dharma, like opening a national treasury.
Grant me only these two manifest proofs of gold:
that all Buddhas of the past have already spoken it, all Buddhas of the future shall speak it, and all Buddhas of the present are now speaking it;
and that Bodhisattvas of the three periods—past, future, and present—have studied it, shall study it, and are now studying it.
The commentary states: Since all Buddhas speak in unison and bodhisattvas all train accordingly, one should know that this is not erroneous;
furthermore, one should recognize the excellence of the jewel, hoping that those who are discerning will see the worthy and strive for equality. What the Sages have said is not in vain.

Second, the specific clarification of the source and flow of the True and Transformation [Buddhas]. This section has two parts: first, clarifying the True Buddha and his transmission of instructions according to the Dharma; second, clarifying the Transformation Buddha who receives them.
The instruction to transmit [the teaching] follows the preceding section on the two [aspects], the first of which raises the subject of his own cultivation and realization:
"I have cultivated practice for a hundred kalpas; this is the name of my mind-ground, and I am called Vairocana.
The commentary states: "I" refers to Vairocana as he is designated according to worldly convention; he is also endowed with the mastery of the Dharmakāya throughout the hundred [kalpas].
"Kalpa" refers to the duration of practice; in reality, it is an immeasurably vast number, though here it is spoken of as "hundreds.

This is the dharma cultivated within the mind-ground. "Vairocana" refers to the fruit sought; because one has practiced this for many kalpas until obstructions are exhausted and virtues are perfected, this fruit is attained.
Although the previous [passage] provided general proof, there may still be lingering doubt; now, by citing a specific personal testimony, it is sufficient to inspire conviction.
This is indeed so; however, because one desires to cause others to practice and study, one first manifests the virtues one has attained oneself.
This refers to those who have already studied as previously explained, while this current section explains what others should study hereafter. Thus, there are two aspects:

causing others to turn toward instruction, and having personally realized the unsurpassed path, using this very means to deliver sentient beings—this is the conduct of a Great Being. The text is divided into two parts.
First, a brief indication:
"You, all Buddhas, turn the wheel of what I have spoken to open the path of the mind-ground for all sentient beings.
The commentary states: "All Buddhas" refers to the thousand Śākyamunis and the hundreds of thousands of billions of Śākyamunis; their transformation proceeds from...
Because the True Arising manifests as the Honored One to transform the lowly, he addresses them as "you. What you have spoken is the ocean of the mind-ground, which flows on in succession;
therefore, it is called "turning" (*vartana*). Because it reveals that which the Dharma belongs to, it is called "I.

All sentient beings are the assembly prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), who are the objects of the teaching. "Opening the path of the mind-ground" refers to the benefit obtained by these objects. "Opening" means—

To awaken and develop the Way is precisely the cause; it causes the Bodhisattva of the Mind-ground to awaken their faculties and develop the categories of precepts, thereby forming the cause for Buddhahood.
Furthermore, it clarifies that these precepts are the path of the Mind-ground, opening it so that one may advance upon it.
Moreover, it clarifies that the Mind-ground possesses a Way, and this Way leads through to the fruit of Buddhahood, opening it up.
To cause this to be practiced means that one takes the fundamental mind as the ground of the mind and takes the precepts as the Way. Second, the extensive exposition.
At that time, from the Lion Throne of radiant celestial light in the Lotus-Womb World (*Padmagarbhalokadhātu*), Vairocana Buddha emitted—
Guangguang addressed the Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotuses, saying, "Take this 'Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Ground of My Mind' and depart.
He then further transformed himself into a thousand billion Śākyamunis and preached this 'Chapter on the Superior Dharma-Gate of the Ground of My Mind' in succession for all sentient beings.
"You all should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and practice it with a single mind."

The commentary states: "At that time" refers to the moment of receiving the transmission from the Buddha. "The Lotus-womb Treasury World" (Padmagarbha-lokadhātu) is the supporting land, meaning the realm upon which it relies.
This refers to the fundamental Great Lotus-womb Treasury containing seeds, as well as all its various merits;
thus it is called the "Treasury. The phrase "majestic below" clarifies the supporting seat and canopy, specifically distinguishing the types of supports. "Lion" [refers to the lion throne].
As for "the seat," it is so called because the Buddha, seated there, is able to subdue Māra, is fearless, and definitively proclaims the Dharma, just like a lion;

thus, the seat upon which a lion sits is named a "lion-seat" (*siṃhāsana*), according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Regarding "celestial light" (*divyāloka*), it means that all the heavens consist of jewels that constantly emit radiance;
since the seat is made of jewels, it is like celestial light. Alternatively, one may take it to mean "pure light" or "natural light."
The light is the light of heaven; because its radiance is blazing, it is called "majestic" (he-he).

Vairocana Buddha is the Master who transmits the Dharma, which constitutes his primary retribution (zhengbao). As for the emission of light, since the lights are not singular, they are called "lights of light.
The intent behind emitting light is to summon the assembly and to manifest the Dharma; this is why he emits light. In the following text, Śākyamuni likewise emulates this manifestation of the Dharma.

The meaning is as clarified below: regarding the Buddha atop the thousand-petaled lotus, some say this is the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) corresponding to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), while others fear it may not yet be so;

I maintain that it is the *saṃbhogakāya* corresponding to a Bodhisattva of the second stage, because in that stage the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) increases and one beholds a thousand Buddhas.
As for the "one thousand, ten thousand, and hundred million Śākyamunis," these correspond to those prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*).
"The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) also [teaches] all sentient beings" refers to the assembly prior to the stages (bhūmi-pūrva) who are taught by the transformation body.

"Furthermore, it transforms again" means that Vairocana personally transmits it to the thousand *sahasrabuddha* reward-bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), causing those reward-bodies to transmit it to the hundreds of thousands of myriads of millions of transformation Buddhas, and causing those transformation Buddhas to transmit it to the sentient beings prior to the stages; thus, below the "hundreds of thousands of myriads of millions,"...

The lower section is concise and does not elaborate, merely stating "it reaches [the recipient]"; this refers to the sequence of the transmitted Dharma. Regarding the term "sequence," there are generally three meanings:
first, in relation to the Buddha who transmits it, it carries the sense of "ascending" (upward-turning);

second, in relation to the sentient beings being transformed, it ensures they are not abandoned; thus, the text below states: "As long as one understands the words of the Dharma Master, one fully receives the precepts."
These three [points] concern the Dharma-gates transmitted; both the words and their meaning from beginning to end are exactly as taught by Śākyamuni.

You must command those below to receive and practice them, not merely to transmit the words. Because they remain unchanged from beginning to end, it is said: "With one mind. This is a direct exhortation to repay the Buddha and a distant encouragement for future lives.

However, the force of the two characters "Guang" (Light) and "Gao" (Announcement) [in the title]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* or a related text. The final phrase "勢" likely refers to the momentum or implication of the preceding terms.)

Regarding the combination and separation [of the light and the speech]: when combined, the Dharma is expounded within the light; when separated, the speech is uttered after the light. Looking ahead to the explanation below, this corresponds to the latter meaning concerning Śākyamuni.

From here on, the second section clarifies the reception of the mandate and the transmission of the teaching, just as a minister receives an imperial decree and dares to proceed in accordance with its text. (2)
The first part provides a general clarification that there are many Buddhas in all realms—referring to Śākyamuni in the thousands of billions of worlds;
the second part specifically reveals the single Buddha of this realm—our own Teacher, Śākyamuni. Within the first section on Śākyamuni, there are two parts:

the first clarifies only a single realm, while the latter categorically distinguishes the other directions. Within the former of these, there are three sections: the first concerns rising from one's seat and making offerings.
The Dharma-Recipient was about to take his leave.
At that time, the Buddhas of the Thousand-Petaled Flower, numbering in the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis, rose from their majestic lion thrones within the Lotus-Womb World and each withdrew.
As they did so, their bodies emitted inconceivable light, and all this light transformed into—

The Buddha, at one time, offered immeasurable flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white as an offering to Vairocana Buddha and completed the reception and upholding of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as explained above.

The commentary states: "At that time, it was precisely the transmission of the Dharma by Vairocana. Regarding the phrase "the thousand petals, etc.," this is to be understood according to what precedes.
The text commands that the thousand Buddhas transmit [the teaching] to the ten trillion Buddhas;
this passage clarifies that it is specifically these thousand Buddhas who, having returned to the Pure Land, subsequently transmit it to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation) Buddhas.

Their dwelling together with the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense) Buddhas is a subtle manifestation of the non-obstruction between the two—the *saṃbhoga* and *nirmāṇa* bodies. This same principle applies to the subsequent verses, where they likewise arise from the lion throne.
Because each had their own seat, they each descended from their seats to make way; as they prepared to take their leave, their entire bodies emitted inconceivable light.

As for the two Buddhas’ bodily radiance being like this light, it all manifested immeasurable Buddhas—within each and every ray of light there were immeasurable Buddhas, which constitutes a further transformation. "At one time" refers to the beginning and the end.
"Combined with the immeasurable" means that each and every Buddha individually makes offerings of immeasurable flowers.
"Blue, yellow, red, and white" refers, in order, to the offerings of *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers.
Regarding "and so forth," it is because one honors the Dharma and respects the person [who upholds it] that people are led to revere the Dharma and thus receive and uphold it.
"Having received [the teaching], he upholds it as a treasure to transmit it to those who have not yet awakened; 'concluded' (jìng) means 'fully realized.

This refers to the fact that everything mentioned above—the hearing of the Dharma, taking leave, the manifestation of light and transformations, the offering of flowers, and the reception of the Dharma-gate—has all been fully realized.
Second, he conceals his form, traverses the void, and returns to his original realm."

Each of them vanished from this Lotus-Womb World; having vanished, they entered the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature and returned to their original source world, beneath the Bodhi tree in Jambudvīpa.
The commentary states: "Because there are thousands of billions of differences, it says 'each and every essence and nature,' etc. This refers to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) entered;
*samādhi* is correctly called *samāpatti*, which is translated here as "equipoise" (*samāhita*), because the mind is held in equality, focusing single-mindedly on one object.
Regarding "the essence and nature is empty space": by entering this absorption, one realizes that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely devoid of intrinsic essence, just like empty space.
It is called "space" because the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is fundamentally space-like by virtue of being devoid of self and dharmas;
furthermore, it is called "empty" because the dependent nature (*paratantra*) lacks substantial reality and the imagined nature (*parikalpita*) is entirely non-existent.

Regarding the term "light of flowers," this is because he is about to expound the *Avataṃsaka* and the precepts of the mind-ground. As for "returning to the source," the Jambudvīpa transformation land is Śākyamuni’s original realm.
He went briefly to the Lotus Terrace, hence it is said he "returned to his original [abode]. Jambudvīpa—here translated as "Jambu Continent"—is so named because this tree exists within the continent;
thus the name of the continent was established. As for the "Bodhi Tree," it was originally a Pippala tree;
it received this name simply because the Buddha attained Bodhi beneath it. Nevertheless, according to the principles of the Dharma, he ought to have entered meditative concentration.

Regarding the passage "Emanating from here and disappearing to return there," it should rather read: "Each [Buddha] enters the *tathatā-śūnyatā-kusuma-prabhā-samādhi* from this Lotus-Womb World (*padma-garbha-loka-dhātu*) and disappears;
having disappeared, they return to their respective original source worlds," etc.—this merely requires reversing the order of the phrasing.

Furthermore, based on the previous distinction between the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body) and the *sambhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body), it would be appropriate to state: "The thousand Buddhas return to the Pure [Land]."
The thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas from the earth-world all return to Jambudvīpa in the south;
that they are not mentioned here is because it is not what is required, because the wording and meaning would be inconvenient, and also to manifest their non-duality.

If one were to speak of them upon arrival, then Vairocana Buddha and the thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas would be two yet without distinction. Furthermore, following the example of the eight phases [of enlightenment] below, it is appropriate to proceed accordingly.
The transformation of Māra in the heavens and his subsequent transformation into birth within the Buddha-way are here briefly summarized;
their detailed accounts, including the lineages of transmission and the dharma assemblies, will be expanded upon later, as each preceding section reflects the subsequent ones. Part Three:
The Fulfillment of the Teachings and the Broad Benefit of All Sentient Beings. Section One: Emerging from Samādhi.

He emerged from the Samādhi of the Body-Nature’s Flower-Light of Empty Space. The "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as taught by Vairocana Buddha.
The commentary states that the two characters "exiting" (*chu*) belong to the preceding section, while the text is connected to this present passage; we follow the text here.
There are eleven locations and ten assemblies of dharma-gates; because the first two are combined, the "middle" of the first assembly signifies the beginning. Gold...
Regarding the Vajra Seat: it is here that the Buddha originally attained enlightenment, and now he returns to this very seat to preach the Dharma.
When the Buddha appears, [the light] manifests; when the Dharma perishes, it vanishes. Now only one part remains.

As for the "King of a Thousand Lights," it is because the seat is adorned with radiant light that is manifold and supreme, and because the Buddha emits many superior rays of light. Furthermore, it is as the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, emits [light].

Regarding the reason why the first meaning is superior: the "Hall of Sublime Light" (*Miaoguang Tang*) is described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as the "Hall of Universal Light," which is composed of jewels that emit wondrous radiance such that there is nowhere it does not illuminate. Furthermore, from within this hall, inconceivable light is emitted, pervading the ten directions.
However, because this [location] is situated only a few *li* from the Bodhi tree, it is not what is being referred to here.
This means that beneath the tree there is this hall. Since it is said that [the worlds] reach as far as the natural [realm], it is not stated that there are ten world-oceans;
for the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that outside the Flower Treasury World (*Huāzàng shìjiè*), there is one ocean in each of the ten directions.
Furthermore, all world-oceans are established through ten kinds of matters; yet, because they horizontally encompass many types and vertically contain many levels, [they are so described].
Since the *dhātu* (realm) is both profound and vast, it is designated by the name "Ocean. In the second assembly, the one called Śakra is fully named Śakradevendra;
this is translated as "Capable Lord of Devas" (*neng tiānzhǔ*), because he is capable of performing skillful transformations as the Lord of Devas.
He is the lord of the thirty-three [gods] atop Mount Sumeru. Regarding the "palace" (*gōng*), the *Erya* states: "A chamber is called a *shì* (room/palace)."

The palace is magnificent, vast, and spacious beyond full description. As for the "Ten Abodes," these are the Abode of Initial Resolve, the Abode of Cultivating the Ground, and so forth, up to the Abode of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).
Regarding the "Flame Heaven" mentioned in the third assembly: its full name is *Suyāma*, which means "Joyful Time.
This is because they experience pleasure according to the seasons. Furthermore, this heaven uses the opening and closing of lotus flowers to distinguish day from night.
Because it is night, it is further said that the blooming of red lotuses constitutes the day and the blooming of white lotuses constitutes the night.

The "Ten Practices" (daśa-caryā) refer to the stages from "Joyful" (*pramuditā*) up to "Reality" (*tathatā*). Regarding the "fourth heaven among the fourth assembly," this refers to the fourth heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In the Sanskrit language it is called Tuṣita, which here means "Contented with Little Desire" (*alpeccha-saṃtuṣṭa*); it is the stage of the final body (*paścima-deha*).

Because the Bodhisattva skillfully transforms and guides those celestial lords, the tenth dedication is "Protecting All Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings," extending even to the immeasurable equality of the Dharma-realm.

In the fifth assembly, regarding the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati-deva*), the full name is the Heaven of Enjoying Emanations; they delight in their own emanations as palaces and so forth, thereby bringing themselves joy.
The ten dhyānas of delight refer to the dhyāna of renunciation, the dhyāna of associating with virtuous friends, and so forth, up to the dhyāna of supernormal clarity (*abhijñā-vidyā*).
Regarding the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven mentioned in the sixth assembly, its full name is the Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin;

it signifies the state of attaining mastery over the enjoyment of all things through transformation. The ten stages (*bhūmi*) are namely: the Joyful (*pramuditā*), the Stainless (*vimalā*), and so on.

This extends up to the seventh assembly, such as the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), where the practitioner of *dhyāna*—here fully termed *dhyāna*, translated as "meditative concentration" (*samādhi*)—is established because this is the beginning of the four *dhyānas* of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the "ten vajras," it means that one has awakened to the fact that all phenomena of the three periods of time are entirely without remainder;
thus, upon the fulfillment of these ten stages (*bhūmis*), one attains the state of Buddhahood and acquires the [ten] vajras.
When one is firmly established in meditative concentration and gives rise to these ten mental states, they illuminate the bodhicitta so that it turns without obstruction;
because it cannot be destroyed by worldly paths and can destroy all obstructive dharmas, this stage is called the "Vajra Mind," and it is not the mind of dedication prior to the stages.
That [previous stage] refers to the ability to subdue the two parts when about to enter the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Regarding the "separate obstacles" (*pṛthag-āvaraṇa*), this refers to that which is capable of destroying all defilements of conceptual signs (*nimitta*) as one is about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood;

thus, while the terminology is slightly similar, the underlying meaning differs. Furthermore, since the coarse and subtle levels are distinct, there is no room for doubt regarding the statement in the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).

As for the ten kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) mentioned in the eighth assembly, according to the *Sugati-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (or *Śīla-samvara-sūtra*), these range from the patience of nature (*prakṛti-kṣānti*) and the patience of being difficult to endure (*duḥsaha-kṣānti*) up to the patience of tranquility (*upaśama-kṣānti*).

Regarding the ten vows in the ninth assembly, the *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra* states that when a bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment, they take great compassion as the foremost and give rise to ten correct vows:

"May my roots of goodness throughout the three periods of time be universally bestowed upon all sentient beings and dedicated toward the fruit of Buddhahood," up to "being protected by dhāraṇīs," and so forth. Regarding the tenth assembly, [the section on] Māheśvara...
"Ruo" (羅) is fully transcribed as *Mahesvara-deva*, which means "Great Sovereign Lord" (*Maheśvara*).

He is the king of the fourth dhyāna and the lord of the Sahā world-system, for he governs all the devas. "Palace" (*gong*) refers to the great palaces that manifest spontaneously according to his will;
the meaning of the "ground of the mind" is as previously explained. The "Dharma-gate" is precisely the Bodhisattva precepts.

This precept is the dharma practiced within the Bodhisattva’s ground of the mind; because it enables one to emerge from the realm of birth and death and enter the realm of nirvana, it is called a "gate.
Thus, practice serves as the gate. Even if the teaching were taken as the gate, one could likewise transcend the suffering of the three realms;
however, while the distinction lies in the means and the object of expression, the underlying intent remains consistent. Such is this Dharma-gate of the ground of the mind.
Because it originates from the Pure Land of the Reward Buddha, it points to Vairocana within the Lotus Treasury as its fundamental source.
According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the seven locations and nine assemblies do not extend beyond the single heaven of Nirmāṇarati within the Desire Realm;
thus, the Bodhi tree and the Hall of Light must certainly be distinct. Among these, the Dharma gates are for the most part expounded by Bodhisattvas, and the teachings so expounded—

The subsequent categories will be distinguished according to other regions.
The remaining billions of Śākyamunis are likewise thus, without duality or distinction, as explained in the "Chapter on the Wise Kalpa" (Bhadra-kalpika-parivarta).

The commentary states that this section is divided into two parts: first, the formal classification of the commonality of their assemblies and locations, stating that in principle they are without duality or distinction.
The location where this teaching was given can be known from the subsequent text.

second, manifesting birth in the human world through the power of his merit to benefit sentient beings; and third, the universal injunction for all conscious beings to accept [the teachings] equally.
First, regarding the present occasion:
At that time, after Śākyamuni Buddha had first appeared from the Lotus Treasury World in the east and entered the celestial palace to preach the *Māraparivarta-sūtra*, he [resumed his teaching].
The commentary states: *Śākyamuni* means "Able Benevolent One" (*Nengren*) and "Silent Sage" (*Jimo*).

Because he does not abide in either nirvana or saṃsāra, his initial manifestation in the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*) refers, in terms of reality, to the first arising of the awakened mind; in terms of its aspect, it is the place where the mind is first established without beginning.

In terms of the perfect [teaching], it is the place where the ten bodies are first perfected and the mind of true awakening is initially accomplished. This flow proceeds from the source, as transformation arises spontaneously from the True.
Because it follows the conventional flow, the current scriptural text first suppresses its original basis;
since those coming from the East are said to be from this world-system [Saha], the underlying intent is that they come from the pure land of the Reward Buddha (*vipākabuddha*).

Herein, the text mentions only the Flower Treasury World-System (*kusumagarbhadhātu*) as a whole and does not specify a "pure land," just as previously demonstrated to manifest unimpededness. If one takes what is symbolized, the East presides over spring and the emergence of life.

The primary manifestation of birth arises from the True [Dharmakāya] to initiate transformation; this is its beginning. As for the "Palace of the Heavenly Kings," it refers to the sixth heaven of the Desire Realm.
Regarding the mention of "Māra" and others: *Māra* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "the Slayer," or "Evil Intent," or "Envy.
This refers to one who does not rejoice in the good and severs the wisdom of others. Thus, when the Buddha was about to descend to be born, he manifested [this form].
Having attained perfect enlightenment, he proclaimed and disseminated the True Dharma to transform the ignorant masses. Because those heterodox ones were contrary to this, he first subdued them;
because they heard his words and submitted, it is called the "Sutra on the Mara Receiving Transformation.

This should be this precept, or perhaps it refers to the very beginning of the future [eons], where it says, "At that time," meaning at such times as these. Question: The *Buddhacarita* and other texts state that [the Buddha] was about to attain perfect enlightenment.
Now, regarding the "subduing of Māra": how is it that he subdues Māra in the heavens above yet attains Buddhahood below?
The answer is: the subduing in the heavens is the actual subduing; the subduing beneath the tree is a manifested display.

Thus, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that when he was about to achieve perfect enlightenment, he emitted light to summon Māra, and having subdued him, he sent him away. Other accounts say various things, but these are likely not [the definitive version].
The Righteous One thus subdues Māra through ten kinds of intentions, as explained in the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra*.

Second, regarding the descent of his virtues to appear among humans to benefit sentient beings, there are three sections in the initial text: first, descending to birth and attaining enlightenment; second, transmitting the Dharma to benefit sentient beings;
and third, the benefits obtained by those born. Now, the first [section].
I shall descend to be born in the southern continent of Jambudvīpa, in the kingdom of Kapilavastu; my mother’s name shall be Māyā and my father’s name Śuddhodana;
my own name shall be Siddhārtha; at the age of seven I shall leave the home life, and at thirty I shall attain the Way, and I shall be called Śākyamuni Buddha.
The commentary states: "Descending to be born" refers to the manner of entering the womb. This is intended to refute the gods' calculation that things are eternal;
for if even superior beings pass away, how could others remain? By this means, they are exhorted not to be negligent again.
*Kapilavastu* is his birthplace; its local name is *Kāpilavastu*, which means "the abode of the yellow-haired seer."
The city of Kapilavastu (translated as "White-Pure") was originally the dwelling place of the four brothers, including King Śuddhodana;
because it was established there, the name of the city became the name of the kingdom. Māyā means "Great Art" (Mahāmāyā).

According to the *Pūrva-yoga*, Śuklodana had eight daughters, the youngest of whom was Bhṛkuṭī (translated as "Worthy"), who was destined to give birth to a holy son. When Śuddhodana heard this, [he sent messengers to request her hand].
The elder and younger sisters of his stepmother—six in all—became wives to his three younger brothers.
The eldest was named Prajāpatī (translated here as "Mistress of Beings"), who was the Great Artificer (Mahāmāyā) and the mother who gave birth to the Buddha;

she passed away seven days after his birth and was reborn in the heavens as a goddess, the Mistress of Beings, and is now known as his maternal aunt. As for "Siddhārtha," it is fully called *Sarvārtha*.
*He-rat-a-si-ta* (Hralta-siddha) means "One Who Accomplishes All Aims" (*Sarvārthasiddha*), because there is nothing—whether mundane or supramundane—that he does not understand;
this represents the aspect of his renunciation at the age of seven. His attainment of the Way at thirty represents the aspect of his enlightenment.

Furthermore, it is said that he renounced the world at nineteen or twenty-five and attained enlightenment at thirty-five; however, the account of his renunciation at seven is based on what was seen or heard.
There may be differences due to errors in transmission or translation; however, while various holy teachings speak of eight phases, here there are only three:

first, the single phase of the infant, which is subsumed under "entering the womb," as the text says he was "born below"; second, the single phase of renunciation at age seven, which is not called "childhood" but rather "renunciation";
and third, the practice of austerities, which is included within "renunciation"; next follows the teaching of the Dharma, which is the "turning of the wheel of Dharma."

The wheel of the True Dharma has arisen and transformed the world; it does not speak of *nirvāṇa*. Its completeness and deficiencies, its separation and correspondence, can be fully understood through this [principle];

the rest of the text may be known accordingly. Section Two: The Transmission of the Dharma for the Benefit of Sentient Beings. Part One: The Greatly Awakened One’s vast compassion has already bestowed manifold transformations.

From sitting upon the Vajra-flower Radiance King Throne at the site of the tranquil place of enlightenment, up to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara,

The commentary explains: "The site of the tranquil extinction of the Way" (śānta-mārga-maṇḍala) refers to the place where the Buddha attained the Way, termed a *maṇḍala*.
Because birth and death have been extinguished, it is called "tranquil extinction"; this is the Bodhi tree. The ten dwelling places have been briefly touched upon as previously explained.
Because there are two ends, it says "up to" (*yāvat*). At that time, the Buddha observed below to clarify the reason for the name of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.

This means that because the Brahma-canopy and the lattice-holes differ in size, shape, and form—being square or round—and because the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) and the sentient world (*sattvaloka*), as well as their mental forms, are likewise diverse, the Buddha’s teachings are applied to them accordingly;
thus, there are distinctions such as the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles. It is on this basis that the name *Brahmajāla Sūtra* was established. This is the meaning.
Thus, among the ten previous assemblies, the first is the world that was taught, while the latter nine are the Dharma gates that were taught;
subsequently, the vertical progression of the coming and going is clarified.
I have now come to this world eight thousand times for the sake of this Sahā world, sitting upon the Vajra-flower Radiance [seat].

The commentary states that "eight thousand times" may vary by one or two and need not be an exact number; it is what the Sahā world can endure.

"Endurance" is as it is commonly discussed; however, the evils of the five turbidities are not like those of the Sahā world. The Great Sage bestows compassion and frequently grants blessings until the end.

Hereafter, the same applies. Any errors are the fault of the translator. Subsequently, the masses of deluded beings struck upon the Sage, and responding to their resonance, they came once more.
Furthermore, descending from the Palace of the Heavenly King to the Bodhi tree beneath Jambudvīpa,
he preached for all sentient beings upon this earth— ordinary persons and those shrouded in the darkness of ignorance—

the single precept of the Radiant Vajra-Jewel Precept, which is constantly recited within the mind-ground of the original Vairocana Buddha at the moment of his first aspiration; it is the source of all Buddhas and all...
The seed of the Buddha-nature, the fundamental source of Bodhisattvas, exists within all sentient beings;
all consciousness, form, and mind—whether emotional or mental—all enter the realm of the Buddha-nature.
The commentary explains that this section is divided into four parts: first, clarifying the location reached—the place of attaining enlightenment where he himself transformed the realm of Māra;

second, from "for this purpose" onwards, clarifying the intended recipients; third, identifying those on the ground as distinct from those in the heavens to avoid confusion with the ranks of the holy, and labeling those who lack even minor merit as "ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*);
and fourth, designating those who are dull-witted, deluded, and confused as "darkness of folly. Alternatively, [the text continues...]

"All sentient beings on the earth" refers to ordinary persons of the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita-bhūmi*), who are people shrouded in the darkness of ignorance—those belonging to the ranks prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). This "on the earth" does not exclude those in the heavens;
however, by excluding them, it emphasizes the threefold teaching of the source. It clarifies that when Śākyamuni was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, regarding these three...
Among the forty mental states of the stages (*bhūmi*), the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*) is precisely that which upholds this precept.

Because this precept is of primary importance, Śākyamuni transmitted it; as it is the foundation for the myriad practices (*sāhasra-pratipatti*), it stands at the head of the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).

Regarding "radiance" (*prabhāsa*) and so forth: these names were established by way of metaphor based on its function. "Radiance" refers to the function of the precept; the precept can support meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and concentration can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*).
"Wisdom-wisdom" (hui-hui) is precisely light; it receives its name from that which it issues forth, and it is also the possession of precepts.

One does not engage in what is unwholesome, just as a person with eyes [sees] because the light of the sun shines upon them. "Lower precepts" are like the sun and moon; regarding the precepts of the Hīnayāna, it is said:
"It is like a person who has eyes," and so forth. The "Vajra Jewel Precept" is a metaphor for the precepts; all evils do not...
Because it can destroy, it destroys all evils; furthermore, light and vajra both pervade essence and function—contemplate this.
Regarding the phrase "the source of all Buddhas," it should be read as the character *yuan* (源), meaning "the beginning" or "the first.
This is because one becomes a Buddha or Bodhisattva by virtue of receiving the precepts; thus, following the path, one relies upon the first step. Therefore, the *Śīla-sūtra* says, "For example..."

Just as a person whose feet are destroyed is incapable of traveling anywhere, so it is with one who has violated the precepts: they cannot be born among gods or humans, let alone attain the state of a Buddha or a Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, regarding the three bodies (trikāya) of a Buddha, these are attained from within the three categories [of beings];
thus, the term "source" (*yuan*) may be applied here, for the pure precepts of the three categories (*tri-saṃvara-śīla*) are the fountainhead of the three bodies. Therefore, the Bodhisattva...
Because one cultivates and realizes the fruit of the three bodies (*trikāya*), it is also regarded as the source; since this source is the most primordial, the character "original" (*ben*) is added.

Alternatively, it may be identical to the One. Regarding the nature of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), there are two kinds: first, the nature of principle (*li-xing*), which is the *tathāgatagarbha*; second, the nature of practice (*xing-xing*). The nature of practice is further divided into two:
first, the seed-nature abiding in its original nature (*prakṛtisthagotra*), which is inherently present by the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*); [the second is the acquired nature].
There exists within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) a single category of continuity, which is the nature formed by habituation (*vāsanā*).
This refers to the seeds of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state that increase in their essential nature after one has generated the Great Resolve (*mahācitta*). "Seed" carries the meaning of a cause;
because this rational nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) differs from wood or stone, and because it relies on the fundamental seeds to attract manifest habituation, one thereby attains Buddhahood.
The title "Seeds" refers to the four types of sentient beings. What follows below clarifies the intention behind the statement that all beings possess Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
This intention is as follows: because Bodhisattvas possess Buddha-nature, they uphold the precepts; by upholding the precepts, they attain Buddhahood.
You, too, possess Buddha-nature and can likewise uphold the precepts to equal the rank of the superior beings (*uttamapuruṣa*). However, regarding the aforementioned "Buddha-nature":

"This is the nature of practice; the nature of practice is precisely the precepts. This statement means that the Buddha-nature is the nature of principle (*li-xing*). The nature of principle is not the precepts.

The meaning is the same, though the phrasing differs; be careful not to confuse them. Regarding "all consciousnesses" and so forth, this explains the characteristics of being capable of receiving the precepts:
"consciousness" refers to the seventh consciousness, "mind" refers to the preceding six [consciousnesses], and "form" refers to the five sense organs (*indriya*) and their physical bases.
The "abiding mind" (*citta-sthiti*) is the eighth consciousness; when these [factors] are combined, they are called "sentient beings.

Regarding what constitutes "sentient" and "mental," among the aforementioned sentient beings, one does not distinguish between high and low or beauty and ugliness; rather, all who possess sentience and possess a mind are included in this category.

As for "precepts" (*śīla*), they are able to prevent wrongdoing and apply universally to the three types of action (*trividha-karman*); because they encompass both the objects of restraint and the capacity for restraint, they are so named.
Ru further said: "Among the three clusters of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*), one is named 'entry' (*praveśa*) because it gathers in sentient beings.
According to my own understanding, all sentient beings possess the same single nature; however, due to habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), there exist seeds of active nature.

Therefore, by universally bestowing the ritual precepts (*vidhi-śīla*), they will necessarily enter into the precepts of nature (*prakṛti-śīla*). These precepts of nature are precisely the seeds cultivated by the ritual precepts."
Because one attains Buddhahood by means of this, it is called "Buddha-nature"; "nature" here carries the meaning of "cause.
To be included within this stream is what is meant by "entering. Is it not likewise so for the benefits obtained by those born later?
Because there is always a cause for "the constant presence of the future" (*dang-dang chang-you-yin*), there is the eternally abiding *dharmakāya* of the future.
The commentary states: "The future" (*dang*) refers to that which is yet to come; because what is to come is not singular, it is called "the constant presence of the future.

That which is the "always-present cause" is the Bodhisattva precepts. This means that because the initial resolve is firm and resolute, having both a beginning and an end, there is a cause present in every lifetime.

That which is the eternally abiding *dharmakāya* is the fruit of the precepts (*śīla*). Because it is realized stage by stage throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it is called "the ever-abiding" (*dangdang*).
Furthermore, both the precepts and the *dharmakāya* each have three aspects: because the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint precepts) serves as the cause, one dwells in the *tathatā-dharmakāya*;
because the *kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts for gathering wholesome qualities) serves as the cause, one dwells in the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body).

Because the morality of gathering beings (*saṃgraha-śīla*) serves as the cause, one abides in the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). Since these are not identical to one another, the term is repeated in each case.
As for the statement that they are "eternally abiding" (*nitya*), it means that their continuity is unceasing and immutable; thus, these three bodies of dharma are all eternally abiding.
Alternatively, my own view is this: if one possesses the morality [of gathering beings] as the cause in every lifetime, one will necessarily abide eternally.

This is the Dharma-body. Regarding the relationship between cause and effect, the speed [of attainment] varies according to the different categories of human beings; therefore, it is called "the appropriate for each" (dang-dang).
Hereafter, all sentient beings who possess consciousness should universally uphold this.
Thus, these ten *prātimokṣas* emerge from the world; they are the Dharma-precepts and belong to all [beings] throughout the three periods of time.
Sentient beings receive and uphold it upon their heads.
The commentary states: *Prātimokṣa* is translated here as "Individual Liberation Precepts.

Because once the prohibitions have been established, the dharma of the precepts resides within one's person, and by individually preventing what is non-virtuous, one attains liberation. This is explained in detail below. Regarding "in the world":
Vairocana recited and transmitted it to Śākyamuni; Śākyamuni, receiving these teachings, spread them among humanity. Therefore, regarding this Dharma-precept:
the precepts possess rules and regulations, and the precepts are themselves the Dharma. Because the Dharma can prevent what is non-Dharma, that which is non-Dharma is the precept.

Thus, at the end of the three periods [of time], he exhorts its upholding. The intent behind the Buddha’s transmission is to moisten all beings with the fruits of holiness; since these fruits arise from this, [one must uphold it].
Since it has been attained, it should be received and upheld upon the crown of the head; the intention is that all sentient beings alike ought to receive and uphold it.

Because the phrasing was not fully expressed, it is fundamentally for the sake of sentient beings who possess the Buddha-nature; since the precepts emerge from the precepts, they accord with reality and should be upheld.
From here below is the second section, the verse text, which has two parts: first, the introduction stating what will be presented; second, the actual verses. Here is the first part:

"I shall now, for the sake of this great assembly, again expound the Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of Precepts, which is the fundamental source and intrinsically pure nature of the precepts for all sentient beings."
The commentary states: "Repeating" refers to the previous eight thousand repetitions, and it also refers to the prose (*gadya*) itself.
Regarding the "ten inexhaustible treasuries" (*daśākṣayakośa*): the number ten signifies perfection, and the meaning reveals inexhaustibility;

because they encompass all things, they are called "treasuries. As for the phrase "all sentient beings, etc.," it should be stated as: "the self-nature precept (*svabhāva-śīla*) of all sentient beings is the source of purity."
"Purity" means that from the very beginning, all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) have been dissociated [from it]; thus, although it appears defiled, it is not defiled.

Therefore, for those who now uphold the precepts, because their nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ, they only then achieve accord with the Dharma; otherwise, all efforts would be in vain.
Only when both nature and characteristics are pure does one attain Buddhahood. Alternatively, since all things possess their respective portions, it is said "all."
Regarding the statement that "the original source of sentient beings' precepts is intrinsically pure," this is because the nature of the precepts is like empty space.

Thus, the subsequent text says: "Having conditions, they are not without cause. Since they belong to the category of causes, they carry the meaning of emptiness; they also constitute wholesome qualities (*kuśala-pakṣa*). In the following formal verse, there are two parts:
first, the verse on the True Buddha’s bestowal of instructions; second, the verse on the Transformation Buddha’s transmission. Within the former:
The first of the four [aspects of] retribution manifests from the Truth.
I, now as Vairocana, sit upon the lotus pedestal; upon the thousand petals surrounding me, there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis.
The commentary states: That which manifests and that which is manifested are mutually [related]. *Sāmbhogika* (Enjoyment Body) refers to the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
"Direction" (*diś*) has the meaning of "beginning" and "correctness. The "lotus pedestal" symbolizes that which is realized as being free from defilement and endowed with virtuous qualities.

Regarding "surrounded on all sides" and so forth: it means that on the four sides of the true Buddha, there are one thousand lotuses surrounding him; this refers to the other-enjoyment body (*parasambhogakāya*).
Each sits according to their respective place; this corresponds to the body of a Bodhisattva of the Second Bhūmi. Regarding the phrase "appears again," it is because of a further repetition.
Since [the Buddha] has already sat upon the flower as Vairocana, looking back from that state, this is the second repetition;
hence it is said "again. These two transformations rely upon the retribution-body to be accomplished.

One flower contains ten billion lands; in each land is a Śākyamuni, each sitting beneath a Bodhi tree, simultaneously attaining the Way of Buddhahood. Thus, there are thousands of billions of Śākyamunis. Commentary:
The first verse clarifies what is manifested by a single flower. Regarding "one flower" and so forth: it refers to one four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*).
One billion sets of four continents constitute one "retribution Buddha" realm; thus it is said that "one flower contains one billion lands.
Because a single Śākyamuni appears in the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa) of each land, it is said that "there is one Śākyamuni per land," thereby resulting in one billion Śākyamunis.
Regarding the phrase "each sits [upon a lotus]," this means that each [Śākyamuni] resides individually in the Southern Continent of their own respective realm.
Because he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment beneath the *pārijāta* tree simultaneously, without any sequence of before or after, it is called "at one time.

The phrase "thus, hundreds of thousands of millions" refers to other flowers; since a Buddha within a single flower can manifest ten billion Śākyamunis, the same applies to the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine Buddhas, thus totaling hundreds of thousands of millions—or perhaps simply ten billion.

Question: If the Buddha of the land is a Great Nirmāṇakāya (Great Transformation Body), why is he described as a Saṃbhogakāya (Enjoyment Body)? Answer: It is simply that when taken collectively across the thousand petals, he is the Saṃbhogakāya;
however, if discussed individually for each one, he is indeed a Great Nirmāṇakāya. Question: If that is so, how can the Great Nirmāṇakāya be identical to that [Saṃbhogakāya]? Answer:
It is simply that when each one is clearly manifested individually, it is what is seen through the power of preparatory application (*prayoga*); thus, each is a "thousandfold" Great Nirmāṇakāya.

The thousand petals collectively describe the extent of what is perceived in the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*). Its magnitude constitutes the essence of the Great Transformation (*mahā-nirmāṇa*), and its meaning is not different;

it is merely that what is perceived varies according to the faculties of the assembly. Thus, the Lotus-Pedestal Treasury (*padma-kośagarbha*) is the self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*), while the pervasive thousand petals are the other-enjoyment (*parasaṃbhoga*).
Within each single petal are ten billion lands, which constitute the great transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). There are one thousand such [transformation-bodies].

The "one hundred million Śākyas" refers to the small transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). According to this principle, the aforementioned phrase "one thousand, one hundred, and ten million Śākyas" encompasses these two types of transformations, as both are transformations that respond to those below the stages of the bodhisattva grounds;

they are mentioned together because they share these common characteristics. If one follows the *Chuanfa* (Transmission of the Dharma), the self-enjoyment body transmits [the teaching] to the other-enjoyment body, and the other-enjoyment body transmits it to the two types of transformation bodies—the great and the small.

The two transformations, great and small, are transmitted to ordinary beings prior to the stages of the grounds; this can all be seen by examining the preceding text. Third, regarding the approach to the source to hear the teaching:
the Dharmakāya Vairocana and the thousands of billions of Śākyamunis each receive hosts as numerous as motes of dust.
All come together to my presence, To hear me recite the Buddha’s precepts; The gate of ambrosia is now opened.

*Commentary:* The first line refers to the True Buddha (*bhūta-buddha*) who is the destination. The second line refers to the Transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) who are the agents of the journey.

The third line clarifies that the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Transformation Buddhas brings the assembly along; it does not necessarily mean they carry them physically in their palms. The fourth line clarifies that both the leader and the followers arrive together.
Because it originates from the Buddha, one must go [to receive it]; for those of inferior faculties or those who have not heard it, it is encompassed by the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) Buddha.

The second phrase concerns the formal reception of the precepts; because they are recited by the Buddha and are the cause of Buddhahood, they are called "Buddha-precepts. The final phrase clarifies the benefits of the recitation of the precepts.
Since there are two meanings to "ambrosia" (*amṛta*), it is used as a metaphor for the three types of precepts, which can eliminate hunger.
Thirst [for the Dharma] brings relief to oneself and others; it encompasses both the gathering of wholesome qualities and the gathering of sentient beings, so that both may obtain benefit.
It can cure diseases and is identical to the *vinaya* (discipline) in its severing of all unwholesome conduct; through this, one attains liberation.

Thus, the precepts (*śīla*) are the gateway, and their transmission, reception, and practice constitute the meaning of "opening. Furthermore, the precepts can give rise to freedom from the heat and affliction of saṃsāra, thereby embracing *nirvāṇa*.
It is for the sake of this purity and coolness that this analogy is employed. Fourth, regarding the transmission and reception [of the precepts]:
at that time, the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis return to their original place of practice;
each sits beneath a Bodhi tree and recites the precepts of my Original Teacher—the ten grave prohibitions and the forty-eight minor rules.

The commentary states: The first three phrases clarify that each of the transformation Buddhas returns to their original station; the latter two phrases clarify that the transmission of the *Prātimokṣa* (Precept Text) is universal.
Regarding the "precepts of the Original Teacher," this refers to the words of Śākyamuni, as one obtains them directly from the True Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "the precepts are themselves the teacher" because they give rise to the Original Teacher, this refers to the words of Vairocana, as evidenced by the text in the *Śāsanānuśāsana-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Buddha’s Last Teaching). Based on... [text ends]
The two explanations regarding the presiding karma can be understood; the characteristics of the ten grave [offenses] and so forth will be explained extensively below.

Regarding the subsequent verse on the transmission of the transformation Buddha, there are two parts: first, citing the assembly of sages to encourage upholding; second, manifesting identity with the Buddha to encourage upholding. This is the first part.
The precepts are like the bright sun and moon, And also like a necklace of pearls.
By means of these, the multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust attain perfect enlightenment. This was recited by Vairocana; I likewise recite it.
You, newly initiated bodhisattvas, Should receive and uphold these precepts upon your heads. Having received and upheld these precepts,
Transmitted to all sentient beings: listen attentively as I recite it. Regarding the explanation of the *Prātimokṣa*, the Treasury of Precepts within the Buddha-dharma:
the first two lines clarify the perfection of the virtue of the precepts; that is, internally they destroy ignorance, and externally they invite respect.

Furthermore, this refers to the two adornments of merit and wisdom. Moreover, because the restraint (*saṃvara*) destroys darkness like the sun, it gathers in sentient beings like the moon to bring them cooling relief;
because it gathers wholesome qualities like a necklace, one adorns oneself with excellence.

The next two phrases clarify the profound and vast utility of the precepts: the upper phrase clarifies their profundity, while the lower phrase clarifies their vastness. The final two phrases clarify the recitation by a Great Being.

Holding the superior to repay the inferior and transforming all through great personhood; the next two lines exhort one toward self-benefit, and the following two lines exhort one toward benefiting others;
the final three lines command that this be received with earnest attention, for otherwise there will be error and no benefit. Thus, the Buddha-dharma distinguishes itself from demons and heretics;
the "Treasury of Precepts" (Śīlaskandha-piṭaka) signifies what is not found in ordinary sutras or treatises; it encompasses all manifold virtues and is established as a "Treasury."
The name "Prātimokṣa" is used because it reveals that this is not a fixed path; however, these six sections arise sequentially, as will be detailed later.
It is shown that [the practitioner] is equal to the Buddha, and thus the exhortation to uphold [the precepts] consists of three parts: first, the exhortation to have faith.
The great assembly, with minds of sincere faith, believe that you shall become a Buddha; I am one who has already become a Buddha—constantly maintain such faith.
The precept-aggregate is already fully perfected. Commentary:
The first phrase exhorts the mind capable of faith not to be superficial; therefore, it says "sincere faith" (*di-xin*). The next two [phrases]...

The first phrase identifies the object of faith; it is like the orchid and chrysanthemum, which differ in season yet share the same fragrance. The latter two phrases distinguish the benefits of faith:
true faith is the purification of the mind, and the purification of the mind is the perfection of precepts.

This is the faith of practice, which alone constitutes true faith—just as the five practices in the *Awakening of Faith* result in the four kinds of faith. Second, there is the exhortation to receive [the precepts].
All those who possess a mind Should all receive the Buddha’s precepts. When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of the Buddhas.
Once their rank is equal to that of Great Enlightenment, They are truly the children of the Buddhas.
Commentary: The first two lines universally exhort [all] to receive [the precepts], which is the meaning of "receiving. What was previously called "should become" refers to speaking to the Buddha.
The essence of the nature is now discussed to clarify the function of the Buddha-nature through the precepts; thus, it is said below:

"If one merely understands the words of the Dharma Master, one fully receives the precepts. This shows that while the phrase "having a mind" refers generally, its specific meaning is distinct. The remaining four lines explain the reason for the exhortation:
even if one can only receive the precepts and has not yet attained Buddhahood, one immediately enters the rank of a Buddha, just as when one becomes a *śrāmaṇera*.
That one does not fall further from the ranks of the Sangha and has few faults and little regret is the way to obtain emolument;
being "equal in rank to those who have already attained Great Enlightenment" refers to the preceding phrase. This merely implies equality in rank, not equality in the functioning of virtue;

it is like a *śrāmaṇera* who, though included in the number of the Sangha, has not yet perfected his observance of the precepts. Those who are truly children of the Buddhas are so because they have received the Buddha-precepts.
Because they are born from the Buddha’s own mouth, they are truly the legitimate heirs, distinguished from those who are outsiders or庶子 (shùzǐ—concubine-born sons). Third, he exhorted them to listen:
"The great assembly shall all listen with reverence and a sincere heart as I recite."
The commentary (*śāstra*) may be understood as follows.
From here on, the second major section, "The Section for the Correct Exposition in Response to Conditions," is divided into three parts: first, a brief preface outlining the origins;

second, the correct recitation in response to the capacities of the audience; and third, the conclusion with exhortations to receive and uphold [the teaching]. Within the first part, there are four sections, the first of which is the preface concerning the time and place of attaining enlightenment.
At that time, when Śākyamuni Buddha had first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment, the commentary states:
from the time he departed and returned, relying on the Truth (dharmatā), he manifested transformation-buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*) who left the Lotus Treasury World to dwell in the defiled lands;
thus, while concealing the realization of the Real, he manifested the attainment of the provisional. This concludes the characteristics of the precepts in the two introductory sections.
The first formulation of the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa is the dharma of filial piety toward one’s parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem;
it is the method of filial devotion to the Ultimate Way. Filiality is called the precept, and it is also called restraint.
The commentary explains that the section on "classification" is divided into two parts. First, the analysis of the characteristics:

regarding the phrase "initially binding," etc., because these are the fundamental precepts that naturally ought to be practiced, they are established as such; thus, the initial binding differs from that of the Hīnayāna.

As for the Bodhisattva *Prātimokṣa*, which is formulated at a later time due to transgressions, this indicates that it is not like the precepts of the Two Vehicles or the precepts of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path. Therefore, [the precept of] filial piety...
This refers to the principle of loving respect and obedience; it is precisely this that enables the mind of filial piety and compliance. To clarify the objects of such filial piety:

parents possess the grace of giving birth and raising one, and thus must be served with filiality. For those currently living, one must provide support with all one's strength to inspire the aspiration for the Way (*bodhicitta*).
For those who have passed away, their precepts and virtues provide hidden sustenance, ensuring they are all freed from suffering. Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings...
Since birth is not without one’s parents, once one possesses their benefit, one thereby fulfills filial piety;

furthermore, manifesting the state of powerlessness as a cause for attaining Buddhahood so as to deliver all beings without exception constitutes great filial piety. As for "teachers and preceptors," they are distinguished from other monks because they possess the grace of instruction and guidance;
therefore, one must be filial toward them. The former refers to the parents of the physical body (*rūpakāya*), while this refers to the father of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Furthermore, because one’s mother was the vessel for their previous life, she gave birth to the fruit of that path; thus, the Three Jewels possess the grace of salvation and must be served with filial piety.
This is because it is not without the Buddha that the teachings are bestowed, and not without the Sangha that the Way is propagated.
