As for the Dharma of the Ultimate Path, it is the *tathatā* (Suchness) and the *dharmatā* (Dharma-nature); it is the most supreme among all phenomena.

Because it distinguishes [this practice] from all other phenomena by virtue of its arising, it is called "the Dharma that reaches the Way. Now, to depart from faults and accord with [the truth] is what is named filial piety (*hsiao-shun*).

As for the various other interpretations, they are all not the correct principle. Question: Is it not the case that the teacher and the *saṃgha* are the Jewel of the *Saṃgha*, and the ultimate Way is the Jewel of the Dharma?
Why then do you speak of them again? Answer: Because one receives their instruction directly, they represent the ultimate realization.
Therefore, by opening up from this basis, four kinds of objects are established. Second, regarding the names "Filiality" and "Precepts":

since all sentient beings are one's own parents, if one refrains from committing acts such as killing or stealing against them and instead gives rise to thoughts of compassion and love, one is thereby able to accord with the intent of the Triple Gem and to conform to the Seal of Truth.
It is because such is the principle [of filial piety] that it is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*). "Restraint" means to restrain good so that it is practiced and to restrain evil so that it is severed;
"stopping" (*nirodha*) refers solely to stopping evil. This is why the explicit teachings open while the implicit teachings prohibit.
Thus, both precepts (*śīla*) and restraint are simply different names for filial piety. Based on this, all the sacred teachings are established as filial piety.
Meaning is derived from instruction; characters follow from the written word. If filial piety were not practiced, it would not constitute instruction.

Therefore, the *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "Filial piety is the root of virtue and the source from which instruction arises. Thus, the three sequences [of the text] manifest the oral teachings through their symbolic expressions.
The Buddha immediately emitted immeasurable light from his mouth.
The commentary states: Since Śākyamuni was thus about to transmit [the teaching] to Vairocana, it was likewise for Śākyamuni when he was about to transmit it to other assemblies.
There are two intentions behind this: first, to gather the assembly by universally summoning those with whom he has a karmic connection, like the striking of a bell; second, to symbolize the Dharma.
The meaning of the exposition of the Dharma is as clarified below: "Immeasurable" refers to a vast number. At that time, four assemblies gathered to listen and receive [the teaching]:
a great multitude of hundreds of millions of bodhisattvas, the eighteen Brahmā heavens, and the sons of the gods of the six heavens of desire. Sixteen...
"Great Kings, join your palms and listen with a sincere heart as the Buddha recites the Mahāyāna precepts of all Buddhas.

The commentary explains that this passage is divided into two sections: first, the assembly gathers; at this time, when the light from his mouth shines everywhere, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of beings—though this number may not necessarily be fixed.
The term "great assembly" (*mahāsannipāta*) belongs to the preceding phrase, whereas the numerical "great" (*mahat*) belongs to the following.
Regarding the phrase "the merit and great texts," although they belong to the subsequent section, their meaning extends throughout all the bodhisattvas above and below.

As for "those who have generated the resolve [for awakening] and so forth, the eighteen Brahmā heavens, etc.," this refers to the fact that there are three heavens in each of the first three dhyānas and nine Brahmā heavens in the fourth dhyāna;

because these serve as leaders, they are specifically mentioned. As for "the six desire heavens," this refers to the Four Heavenly Kings and so forth. As for "the sixteen great kingdoms," it refers to...
This refers to the kingdom of Aṅga and others; according to the meaning of the subsequent text, these should include the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings.

At present, some are omitted, or perhaps they are already subsumed therein without being left out. These beings, seeing the light and knowing that the Buddha was preaching the precepts, were all startled in their respective regions and gathered together at the site of the Way.
With palms joined, they listened with reverence. "Palms joined" means to pay respectful homage.
"To listen with a sincere mind" means to listen attentively. "All Buddhas" refers to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"Mahāyāna" distinguishes this from the Hīnayāna; thus, these are the Mahāyāna precepts taught by all Buddhas.
Furthermore, because these Mahāyāna precepts are the very foundation of all Buddhas, they are called "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle) on account of being the source of the Buddhas.
From here below is the second section: the correct recitation of the text in accordance with the capacities of the audience. This has two parts: first, a general praise of the virtue of the precepts;

second, the specific recitation of the characteristics of the precepts. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, clarifying the profound and wondrous nature of the dharma of the precepts; second, distinguishing the vastness of the capacities for the precepts.

Within the first of these, there are two sections: first, that which is manifested by way of the phenomena; second, the exhortation to practice and study them collectively. Within the first of these, there are two sections: first, manifesting excellence by way of the individuals.
Next is the section on the Manifestation of Radiance, which is superior to the preceding one.

First, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "I shall now, every half-month, personally recite the Dharma-precepts of all Buddhas for you—all you bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds, as well as those in the ten stages of departure, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten adamantine stages, and the ten bhūmis."
The Bodhisattva also recites it.

The commentary explains that this is divided into two parts. First, regarding the "venerable half-month," as for its timing: if it is the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*), it is definitely the fifteenth day;
if it is the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*), it is either the fourteenth or the fifteenth. As for why it is called the "half-month": [it is because...]

Regarding the person, there is neither satiety nor forgetfulness; regarding the manifestation of the Dharma, the dark half of the moon—the darkness—is exhausted and the white half—the light—is perfected.

This is what is manifested: the exhaustion of evil and the perfection of the gathering of good through the restraint of the *vinaya*. The single precept that gathers in all living beings encompasses these two aspects.

As for the "Dharma-precept," the precept itself is the Dharma because it pervades both teaching and practice; thus, when the Buddha recites the Buddha-precepts, the subject and the object are both supreme.
Second, "you all" below refers to the assembly; the term "all" is used to encompass the four subsequent categories of those who have resolved their minds (*cittotpāda*).

Those in the stage of the Ten Faiths (*śraddhā*) are called "those who have resolved their minds," as they have not yet attained a formal stage. Those in the Ten Abidings (*vihāra*) are called "those who have set out" (*prasthita*), because this is the beginning of the three sages (*trividha-ārya*).
Those in the Ten Practices (*caryā*) are called "those who are nurturing," because they cultivate roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). [The character] "gold" [indicates the Ten Dedications].
The "firm" refers to the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), for they are solid and indestructible; thus the ten stages (*bhūmi*) may be known.
Second, the section on the excellence of the manifest light has two parts: first, that which manifests, and second, that which is manifested. Now, the first part.
Therefore, the light of the precepts issues from the mouth; it has a cause and is not without a reason. Thus, this light is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black.
The commentary states: "Therefore" refers to the sequence of preceding and succeeding points. The meaning is that when the time arrives and one wishes to recite the precepts, for this reason...
Regarding "the light of the precepts emitted from the mouth": the light symbolizes the precepts; it is not that the precepts are the light itself.
As for the light emerging from the mouth, it signifies that the Buddha himself recites [the precepts] and exhorts all sentient beings to recite them as well.

Because the true sons who possess the precepts emerge from the Buddha’s own mouth, the phrase "having conditions" and so forth symbolizes that the light produced from the precepts—which arise from causes and conditions—is free from the extremes of existence and non-existence.

It is not merely the five colors; because the manifestations of light are manifold, it is called "light upon light. As for the term "conditioned by causes and conditions" (pratyaya), it means that the precepts arise only through the resonance between teacher and disciple.
Thus, regarding the two aspects of what is expressed in the text, first is the profound and subtle nature of the essence of the precepts (śīla-skandha).
It is neither matter nor mind, neither existent nor non-existent, and not a phenomenon of cause and effect.
The commentary states: "Neither matter nor mind" means it is not matter because it lacks substantial obstruction, and it is not mind because it lacks cognitive discernment.
"Neither existent nor non-existent" means that being produced by causes and conditions, it is both provisional and empty, and furthermore, it is not something grasped as a self-entity.
Because it does not arise through dependent origination, it is not non-existent; because it takes the bodhicitta as its cause, it is not a cause;
because it can bring about the fruit of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), it is not a fruit. Speaking of its essential nature, it is neither Buddha nor Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, it is not a cause because sentient beings attain it and thereby become Buddhas; it is not a fruit because... [the text continues].
Because the Buddha attained [enlightenment] to transform sentient beings, the final character "dharma" (fa) connects with the meaning of all the preceding texts.

It states that by means of this precept-dharma, which is initiated through the provisional causes and dependent conditions, one is able to become detached from the dharmic marks of form and mind, existence and non-existence, cause and effect, and so forth.
Second, the application of the precepts is profound and far-reaching.
This is the fundamental source of all Buddhas, the root of practicing the bodhisattva path, and the foundation for all the sons of the Buddha in this great assembly.
The commentary states: although it is not the fruit, it can serve as the fundamental source of the Buddhas; although it is not the cause, it can serve as [the foundation] of the bodhisattvas.
Although the roots of practice are both neither cause nor effect, they can nonetheless serve as the foundation for the great assembly and others.

Furthermore, because they are not causes, they may be treated as effects; because they are not effects, they may be treated as causes. Since they are not fixed causes, one is able to attain their subsequent effects, thereby encouraging beings to cultivate and study them.
Therefore, the great assembly of sons of the Buddha should receive, uphold, read, recite, and study well.
The commentary states: this intends to cause them to receive and uphold the matter, read and recite the text, and study well the meaning. "Should" (應) means to exhort and encourage these three;
the subsequent section will distinguish the vast and extensive scope of the conditions for the precepts.
Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! Whether they be kings, princes, high officials, ministers, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, the eighteen Brahmā heavens,
the sons of the gods of the six heavens of desire, commoners, eunuchs, male and female libertines, slaves,

the eight classes of spirits and ghosts, *vajra*-deities, animals, or even those who are transformation-beings— provided they understand the words of the Dharma Master, all such persons may receive the Buddha’s precepts.
"Those who have received the precepts are all called the foremost pure ones.
The commentary explains that this section on the divisions has three parts: first, a general indication regarding the precepts;

second, a detailed enumeration by category starting from "kings and others," totaling twenty categories which, when expanded, include even more variations; and third, "humans," such as those like dragons who transform into human form, and so forth.

The disparagement of this [Mahāyāna] by those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) as being difficult to understand can be inferred from the remaining text. Third, regarding the resolution below, which summarizes according to the capacity of the vessel:

thus, while there are people who are incapable, there are also animals whose qualities may be accepted. This is not a matter of evaluating superiority or inferiority based on physical form or species.
Furthermore, one must clearly comprehend the meaning of the text to be called "one who understands the language"; this differs from a parrot, which merely repeats the words it has heard.

Regarding "the first purity," the *Buddhatva-śāstra* (Treatise on Buddha-nature) explains that there are two kinds of purity: first, essential purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), because it is inherently free from the defilement of delusions;

second, purity of appearance (*lakṣaṇa-viśuddhi*), because obstacles are removed through their antidotes. Here, the text refers to the former meaning, hence it says "the first. It further says "regarding the person" (*pudgala*) to clarify [the subject].

Next is the separate recitation of the text concerning the characteristics of the precepts, which has two parts: first, the explanation of the ten grave offenses; second, the explanation of... [the secondary offenses].
Regarding the ten precepts for light defilements (*laghu-mala*) within the preceding [section], each one is established specifically to prevent the three poisons internally.

If the three poisons do not exist, the seven branches [of misconduct] will naturally cease; if the three delusions do not arise, the seven [branches] cannot be transgressed. How much more so when acting in accordance with compassion and wisdom—would such an act be a transgression or its observance?

If one does not rely on the internal state of mind to determine right or wrong, what basis is there for judgment? If they were fixedly assigned to the three types of action (body, speech, and mind), they would be no different from those of the Small Vehicle.

Those who ride upon the Great Vehicle may examine this in detail and clearly discern its merits and defects. Furthermore, these ten precepts, when considered in terms of their manifest characteristics, are exclusively the *vinaya* (restraint);

yet, when discussed in terms of their subtle implications, they also encompass the other two [types of restraint], namely the restraint of overcoming evil and the restraint of promoting good, because they involve both personal practice and instruction of others.

If one does not instruct others, one is not a Bodhisattva. As clarified previously, there are three parts: first, the heading; second, the exhortation to recite; and third, the actual text. First, the heading: the exhortation to recite.

Holding these two points as evidence, the text correctly reveals the subsequent conclusion and exhortation, which refers back to the preceding section in two parts. First, it cites the number and exhorts recitation.
The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddha, saying: "There are ten grave *pratimokṣa* rules.
If one has received the Bodhisattva precepts and does not recite these rules, they are not a Bodhisattva and are not the seed of a Buddha; I, too, shall likewise recite them."
The commentary states: One who is a bodhisattva must necessarily practice the path of the two benefits (*dvayārtha*). If one does not recite [the teachings], one cannot transmit them;

thus the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) will not be accomplished. If it is not accomplished, it ceases with one’s own person alone, and by this means the seed of the Buddha (*buddhabīja*) is forever severed.
Since the practice of a Buddha is not otherwise possible, one is not the seed of a Buddha. Being neither the seed of a Buddha nor a bodhisattva, furthermore, if one does not...
If one hears this yet still cannot attain unexcelled bodhi for oneself, then one is neither the seed of a Buddha nor a Bodhisattva.
My own recitation of these words is precisely to clarify the meaning that those who do not recite them are neither the seed of a Buddha and so forth.

Furthermore, the True Buddha transmits [the Dharma] to the Reward Buddha, and the Reward Buddha transmits it to sentient beings; if sentient beings are unable to transmit it, how can they be called children of the Buddha?
Since the Buddha’s heirs are not barbarians, after explaining the Bodhisattvas, he now cites examples to exhort their observance:
"All Bodhisattvas have studied it, all Bodhisattvas shall study it, and all Bodhisattvas are studying it now.
I have briefly explained the characteristics of the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa; you should study it and respectfully uphold it."

The commentary states: By citing past and present examples to exhort future students, it is shown that those who study and understand must understand the teachings they have received, and those who recite and transmit them must practice and uphold the Dharma they have understood. Since these points are explained extensively below, this section is called a "brief exposition.
Second, according to the actual facts, the ten grave precepts are explicitly revealed and divided into ten sections.
○ First, regarding the precept against taking life: Bodhisattvas take compassion as their foundation, while sentient beings prioritize their physical lives.

Because the preservation of life is paramount, this precept is elucidated first; it differs from the Hīnayāna, which prioritizes the precept against sexual misconduct due to its urgency for renunciation.
The text has two parts: first, the formal announcement to the audience; second, the actual exposition of the precept. This is the first part.
The Buddha said, "O Son of the Buddha.

The commentary explains that regarding the phrase "the Buddha said": if taken in its immediate sense according to the sequence established by the compilers, it refers to the words of Śākyamuni Buddha;

if based on the transmission of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) back to the source, it refers to the words of Vairocana Buddha. Although the root and the branches differ, in reality, both are encompassed.
The "Buddha-sons" (buddhaputra) referred to here are Bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the Great Mind (mahācitta) and received the Great Precepts;

born from the Buddha-dharma and having attained a portion of the Buddha-dharma, they succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas and are thus called Buddha-sons. They are neither ordinary deluded beings nor those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

Although they are designated as "Bodhisattvas" in the context of the offenses and transgressions, the following nine sections are identical to this; therefore, they are not separately categorized thereafter.
The text for the formal presentation of the precepts has two parts: first, the establishment of the precepts to ensure their practice; second, the imposition of offenses for violating prohibitions.

Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the establishment of what should be refrained from; second, the establishment of what should be practiced. The former constitutes the *vinaya* (restraint), while the latter consists of the precepts for gathering wholesome qualities and benefiting sentient beings, which apply to both paths.
Within the first of these, there are two further points: first, indicating the characteristics so that they may be known.

Whether it be killing oneself, inciting others to kill, employing the means of killing, praising killing, seeing it done and rejoicing in it, or even killing by means of incantations—whether through the cause of killing, the condition of killing, the method of killing, or the karma of killing.

The commentary states: the first section clarifies the categories of killing; the second section shows that killing pervades the three types of action, meaning that killing oneself is physical action (*kāyakarman*).
Teaching [another] to kill involves two aspects: first, it is preceded by the two types of volition—those of one’s own mouth and mind, and those that resolve upon the matter for oneself or others;
second, there are two ways of teaching another to kill, namely, commanding them to kill themselves or causing another person to take their life.

Now, a Bodhisattva ought to practice the two benefits (svārtha and parārtha), yet here they instead commit the two harms. Second, regarding the characteristics of the preparatory act (*prayoga*) of killing, "praising" refers to providing an explanation that encourages [the act]. There is a distinction [between these cases].
The "double-doubles" (*saṃsaṃ*) are also of two kinds: praising the person capable of killing, or praising the method employed. Each of these two is further divided into two:
praising [the victim] before they have been killed to incite them to die, and praising them after they have been killed to make them rejoice.

Because all of these involve skillful words used to persuade others toward what is considered beautiful or desirable, they are called "expedient means of separation. What has been clarified above consists merely of such praise.
As for cases such as the execution of Fan Chen by Qianju or the killing of the three scholars by Yanzi—these are instances of skillful means (*upāya*).
These differ from teaching others to kill; the latter is a manifest form of instruction, whereas the former involves hidden harm.

Furthermore, this [category of] "rejoicing in the act" (*anumodana*) is twofold: it refers to rejoicing in the act of killing itself, or rejoicing in the final incantation that brings about the death.
Some [instances] involve merely incanting prayers, while others involve incantation-techniques (*mantra-kauśalya*).

Regarding the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*), the intended meaning is that within the two categories of killing—self and other—there are many varieties of karmic conditions for killing, such as the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) and so forth. Since these modes of killing are too numerous to be enumerated exhaustively, and because killing by means of incantations is the rarest, the text says "up to and including.
The third [point], the instruments of killing (*vadha-sādhana*), refers to the internal mind, which encompasses the three poisons (*triviṣa*).
This means that killing for profit, such as through butchery or hunting, has greed as its cause; retaliating with enmity for enmity has hatred as its cause;

and killing out of ignorance of sin and merit, or out of playfulness or preference, has delusion as its cause. Apart from those instances involving greed or hatred, all acts of killing have delusion as their sole cause.
Regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*), these refer to external objects; they consist of both general and specific types, the specific being extreme poverty and distress.

Occupations (*vṛtti*) refer to the expression of one’s capacities, such as customs and entertainments; these include, in general, the bow and arrow, the sword and halberd, up to falcons, dogs, hands, and feet.

"Dharma" refers to rules and regulations, such as the sinking of a ship or the flash of lightning. "Karma" refers to the act of killing itself—either the actual performance or that which is taken as the object of action.
Whether it serves to honor the self or benefit the family, its higher reaches are universal while its lower applications are restricted; this can be understood through careful reflection.

However, it is only when the first three factors are fully present that this karma is established; if any are lacking, it is not established. Therefore, in the subsequent section on minor offenses (*laghulaghuka-āpatti*), each is separately prohibited.

Furthermore, regarding the sequence of these four—object, intention, application, and completion—if one refers to their actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), the object comes first and the intention follows;

if one refers to the seeds (*bīja*), the cause (intention) comes first and the object follows. Next, the dharma and the subsequent action are fixed and never diverge; all subsequent cases follow this pattern.
Second, the establishment of the precept to bring about cessation: "One must not intentionally kill any living being.

The commentary explains: the first phrase clarifies the object, specifying that the objects to be killed are fully enumerated as nine categories; the second phrase clarifies the mind, [referring to the intention].
Regarding the mind of killing, if one refrains from forming the intention, then all life is equally precious; yet the determination of the mind regarding karma differs.
In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), [killing] animals and the like is considered light karma, whereas [killing] human life is grave.

This is because the Buddha-nature is equal, because there are none who are not one's parents, because one must deeply guard the ground of the mind, and because all phenomena are but mind alone. Question: Why was it stated previously that...?
Question: Is it only when the causes and conditions are fully present that killing is accomplished? Answer: The former [passage] explains how the act of killing is accomplished;
this [passage] defines the specific offense of killing. Therefore, they are not the same. The latter prescribes what ought to be done.
This bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of constant compassion, a mind of filial piety, and employ skillful means to rescue and protect all sentient beings.
The commentary states: the bodhisattva, who is a person upholding the precepts, should give rise to the lower [level] mind capable of rescuing all sentient beings.
The objects to be rescued by one's birth refer to all living beings mentioned above;

among them, those facing death should be rescued with a heart of compassion, those who oppose you should be harmonized with a heart of filial piety, and they should be protected with a heart of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, filial piety may be extended to all, for all are one's parents. Thus it is said.
Thus, compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are simply specific manifestations of filial piety.

As for the arising of the "ever-abiding" [mind], these three mental states must be brought forth and maintained ever-present within one's breast; even in moments of haste or distress, they must not be forgotten for a single instant.

Furthermore, the mind that is thus aroused is like the nature of the ever-abiding itself—namely, the unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) and so forth. Expedient means (*upāya*), however, is not like this.

Because [the body] is subject to decay, or conversely, because it may be harmed; furthermore, although one gives rise to compassion, there is no distinction between self and other, for this does not conflict with the essence of the eternally abiding [Dharmakāya].
This is the great skillful means (upāya): advancing, one does not lose its function; retreating, one does not violate its essence.
One who practices these two benefits without failing in the precepts is a true Bodhisattva. Having ceased the killing of others, one must necessarily [cease it oneself].

"Not doing" is the opposite of the aforementioned categories of killing; furthermore, compassion and so forth are the opposites of the aforementioned causes of killing, while skillful means are the opposites of the auxiliary conditions.
Protecting others is the opposite of the karma of killing. Since the instruments of killing no longer exist, how can the characteristics of killing be established?
Because the unwholesome is overturned to become wholesome, it is called the "precept of collecting wholesome qualities. Subsequently, one incurs offenses by violating prohibitions.
On the contrary, for one who instead kills living beings with a self-indulgent mind and a sense of gratification, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

The commentary explains: "Self-indulgent mind" (*zìxīn*) refers to the state of mind when about to kill; it is difficult to restrain. "Gratification of the will" (*kuàiyì*) refers to the feeling of exhilaration after having completed the killing.

Furthermore, "self-indulgence" implies that the murderous intent is limitless, while "gratification" implies that the act of killing accords with one's desires. "Conversely" (*fǎn*) indicates the opposite of the previous [virtuous] states.
"Self" (*svayaṃ*) carries two meanings: first, while one ought to save living beings, now one harms them—this is the first reversal.
Second, while one ought to teach others according to the Dharma, now one personally practices killing—this is the second reversal. This includes the term "self.
As for the "Bodhisattva," this refers to the aforementioned "Son of the Buddha"; *pārājika* is translated here as "defeat" (*tā-sèng-chù*).
"Place" refers to that upon which the observance or violation of precepts depends; thus, for a bodhisattva, observing the precepts is "self" and violating them is "other.
Since one has now violated the precepts, this is the "place of others. In my view, this likely refers to Avīci;
as Avīci is the dwelling place of those who violate the precepts, it is the most inferior of places, thereby clarifying that all other places are superior. This concerns the offense.
"Zui" (摧) means to destroy. Because one destroys wholesome dharmas, once evil karma has been created, how can there be any wholesome dharma?
Even if seeds of goodness exist, they will not sprout; therefore, it is also called "destroying. Furthermore, the Great Being’s vast compassion is the cause of the precept of mind;

since one is no longer a son of the Buddha, how much more so when one inflicts killing and harm, taking pleasure in it and indulging one's passions? The fault is profound, and thus this [consequence] is bequeathed.

Regarding those who initiate such practices: if they truly embrace compassion as their intent, seeking to eliminate suffering and promote benefit, then even if they commit the sin of killing, they should strive to ensure that life is ultimately sustained;
in cases such as those of the immortal Xu Yu, there would be no fault.

However, for those of mediocre capacity and below, if they cannot be guided to practice this, it is not merely a minor error; rather, acting erroneously will result in great transgression. For this reason...
Gains and losses are prohibited and not permitted; most of the subsequent precepts share this same intent. Second is the precept against stealing.
Because life is sustained by necessities such as food and clothing, this follows immediately after the preceding one.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All sentient beings sustain themselves through food and clothing; if these are plundered or seized, it constitutes [stealing]."

The section on the thief of one’s lifespan has two parts: first, the formulation of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the establishment of the offense for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the formulation of what should be desisted from;
second, the formulation of what should be practiced. Within the first of these, there are two subsections: first, indicating the characteristics so that they may be known.

"If a Buddha’s disciple steals, teaches others to steal, uses expedient means to steal, steals by incantation, or steals through the causes of stealing, the conditions of stealing, the methods of stealing, and the karma of stealing.

The commentary states: The first section clarifies the categories of stealing; the second clarifies the three types of stealing; and the third clarifies the three karmas, which are the same as before, except for the act of teaching others.
This merely clarifies one point. Second, regarding the characteristics of the preparatory stage (*upakrama*) of stealing: this excludes cases where one steals with one's own body or hands;

rather, any taking that is not righteous constitutes the preparatory stage of stealing. This includes using incantations to cause spirits or deities to take [the object], or shifting another person’s mind so that they relinquish it and one takes it oneself—there are many such types. These two have been briefly cited here, as they both pertain to the preceding precept.

Furthermore, there is brief praise and rejoicing. Alternatively, by means of skillful means, one may appropriate the requisites for the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) for those who possess the causes for theft;

this also applies to the three poisons. Regarding greed (*lobha*), it should be understood that although the object is not what one personally requires, one takes it away from another because one does not wish for them to have it, thereby preventing their destitution.
Anger (*dveṣa*) serves as the cause; apart from greed and anger, taking what is not given [is the act].
All [afflictions] have delusion as their cause; yet among these three, greed is most prevalent. Its conditions are not singular, namely:
greed, fear, resentment, habitual practice, and tools for burglary, etc., which may be understood through both general and specific categories. Regarding phenomena (*dharma*), they are norms;
regarding action (*karman*), it is actual performance, or that by which one makes a living. Other meanings follow the previous two. The precepts are established to effect cessation.
"Up to and including the property of spirits and ghosts, the goods of owners, thieves, and all manner of wealth—not even a single needle or blade of grass—may one steal intentionally.

The commentary explains: "First, regarding the objects stolen, the mention of 'spirits and ghosts' and so forth distinguishes the objects according to their respective owners. Regarding "ghosts": [text continues].
Regarding "divine objects" (*śrīmanta*), there are three categories: first, those that are ghosts but not divine, such as items found in ordinary family tombs or objects used in domestic sacrifices;
second, those that are divine but not ghosts, such as the possessions of the Four Heavenly Kings (*caturmahārājika*) and others;

third, those that are both ghosts and divine, namely the objects within various shrines and temples, because they are subsumed under the realm of ghosts (*preta-gati*). Regarding "objects belonging to bandits," there are two interpretations, the first of which is...

If one knows that thieves have seized, abandoned, or hidden property, and takes it; or if one seizes it back from them—this refers to cases where one has already taken what was stolen by others and then robs those others of it.
Now, examining the meaning of the text: if one uses the light to illustrate the heavy, even if spirits and ghosts steal objects, one still may not take them as theft;
how much more so with human property? And taking this as an illustration, one certainly may not take the property of the Triple Gem or any of their wealth.
Regarding "things" (*vastu*): this term distinguishes objects by way of their general categories (*varṇa-jāti*), without excluding specific types such as gold, silk, money, or grain;

hence it says "all. Regarding "even a single needle or a single blade of grass": this distinguishes objects by way of their quantity, showing that they differ from the Lesser Vehicle’s requirement of five *māṣaka* coins.
Thus, the phrase "even unto" (*yāvat*) runs through all three sections; reflect upon this.

"One must not intentionally steal" means that one merely restrains the mind that intends to steal; apart from cases where there is no such intent, the moment one gives rise to the thought [of stealing], one commits an offense.
This differs from the rules of the Hīnayāna, which require the object to be moved from its original location before an offense is established. This is what should be practiced.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of filial piety toward the Buddha-nature, a mind of compassion, and should constantly assist all beings to produce merit and happiness.
The commentary states:

The meaning of "Buddha-nature" is the same as previously explained regarding its permanence; it is merely a difference in name. The names "filial piety," "compassion," and so forth are [the specific designations].

The meaning is the same as "constant" (*nitya*) in that it refers to uninterrupted time; "all" (*sarva*) means it universally encompasses all categories. Although the text speaks only of "humans," it actually includes ghosts and others.
"Merit" (*puṇya*) applies to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); "happiness" (*sukha*) includes both the mundane and the supramundane.

The only difference lies in merit being the cause and happiness being the fruit. As for the term "assistance," it means protection, because one protects those objects; alternatively, it means bestowing them upon others.
Provide them with clothing and sustain them with food and drink; guide them with ritual and music, and demonstrate the Dharma gates.

If one ensures that blessings and joy all assist in the righteous purpose, then by reversing the previous [prohibition], the meaning will be clearly understood. Should one later violate this prohibition, one incurs an offense.
To instead steal the wealth and property of others constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

The commentary states: Since one fails to bestow compassion and charity and instead commits theft, one violates strict prohibitions; how then can such a crime be evaded? One must carefully examine for oneself the distinctions between what is permitted and what is forbidden, as well as the benefits and harms involved.

○ Third, the Precept against Sexual Desire. The *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states: "Although sexual desire does not afflict the minds of other sentient beings, it is a grave offense because it binds the mind.
It is explained next because there is nothing by which one fails to remain in birth and death for immeasurable kalpas.

This section has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the definition of the offense for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections.
This is what must be restrained.
If a disciple of the Buddha engages in sexual misconduct himself, or teaches others to engage in sexual misconduct—even with any woman—he must not intentionally commit sexual acts.

Whether through the causes of lust, the conditions of lust, the methods of lust, or the karma of lust—even with female animals, female devas, female ghosts or spirits, or by engaging in improper ways—he must not do so.
"Sexual misconduct.

The commentary explains that this is divided into three sections: first, it indicates the categories of sexual misconduct; second, it concerns the three types of karmic action through which it is understood;

and third, it shows that one may incite others to commit sexual acts with even their own elder sister-in-law, sons, or daughters. Second, regarding the indulgence in sexual conduct, there is no discrimination made between those who are close or distant, nor between those who are attractive or shameful.

It is said that all women are subject to this rule; as explained below, these women are all prohibited [from sexual misconduct], not only men. This is merely a mutual illustration through the influence of the text.
Furthermore, for now, we take the male as the primary case; if one were to take the female as the primary case, the calculation would be the reverse, which is impossible.
Therefore, regarding sexual misconduct, having excluded cases of force or lack of intention, the offense is incurred as soon as the intent arises.
Unlike the followers of the Hīnayāna who rely on literal facts, they likewise fail to attain bliss.

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that a śramaṇa who engages in sexual intercourse in a dream and subsequently rejoices in it or praises it upon waking will, after death, enter the Padma Hell.
This passage should properly have been placed in the fourth section; its current location is also the error of the translator.
Third, the causes for the requisites of sexual misconduct are also understood to be common to the three poisons.
One may know that there is actually no affection, but merely desires to cause the other to feel shame and thus engages in the act; this has hatred as its cause.

Apart from these two, what is called the condition of delusion (*moha*) is also of many kinds: namely, [the desire for] wealth, status, beauty, artistic skill, cosmetics, rouge, fine silks, and resentment.
"Equal dharmas" refers to those things that are appropriate for one's occupation or those to which one devotes oneself;

these four manifest the objects of lust. Furthermore, looking ahead at the subsequent text, there are ten categories in total: first, animals; second, devas; third, ghosts; fourth, spirits; fifth, other humans;

sixth, one’s mother; seventh, one’s daughter; eighth, one’s elder sister; ninth, one’s younger sister; tenth, one’s female relatives. Because this is a summary, the remaining categories are omitted; hence it is so stated.
Furthermore, reversing the perspective from woman to man, there are five [instances]; as for "non-ways" (*amārga*), the following analyzes the locations of sexual misconduct in two senses:
first, it specifically discusses the lower parts and the mouth of the woman; second, it generally encompasses the mouth and other [orifices] of the man. This establishes what ought to be practiced.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience to save and deliver all sentient beings and bestow the pure Dharma upon them.
The commentary explains: "A mind of filial piety and obedience" means loving and respecting [others] just as one does one's own parents.

Regarding "saving and delivering" and so forth, it means demonstrating the faults of desire, causing them to receive the precepts and other teachings, and leading them to leave the bonds of desire; this is what is called "saving and delivering. This reverses the previous [explanation].
One should consider that violating these two prohibitions constitutes an offense;
however, to instead give rise to sexual desire for all people without distinction— even with animals, or even one's mother, daughter, sister, or other close relatives—
and to engage in such lust without a heart of compassion, constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
The commentary states: Having already committed the fault of being defiled while in a state of purity, one further acts improperly toward one’s mother and others;
by engaging in conduct worse than that of beasts and surpassing even birds and animals, one’s transgressions and accumulated burdens become layered upon one another.

Thus it says, "furthermore," which is an abbreviation for including spirits, ghosts, and so forth. As for the "six relations," these are father, mother, husband, wife, son, and daughter. They are devoid of compassion.
Compassion is the opposite of the above; if one first uses the hook of desire to draw them in and subsequently leads them into the Buddha-way and so forth, there is no fault.

Regarding the fourth precept against false speech, this [precept] binds while that [compassionate act] liberates. The *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states: "It is like [the case of] Chou..."
It is easier to extract a piece of wood from the forest if it is straight; furthermore, because false speech serves as the preliminary means for the three preceding [offenses], it is regulated next.

This section has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the incurrence of guilt for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections:
first, the establishment of that which should be refrained from.

If a Buddha’s disciple personally speaks falsehoods, teaches others to speak falsehoods, uses skillful means to speak falsehoods, or speaks falsehoods through causes, conditions, methods, or karmic actions of falsehood—
even to the point of claiming to have seen what was not seen, or claiming not to have seen what was seen— this constitutes a falsehood of body and mind.

The commentary explains that the four sections first clarify the categories of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). Second, regarding false speech itself, it primarily consists of speech and mind, yet it also includes the body;
this is because one may perform deceptive acts or manifest joy, anger, and so forth. Therefore, the subsequent text says:
"False speech of body and mind. Briefly clarifying the characteristics of falsehood, it refers to such statements as, "I did not enter meditative concentration today," and so on.
Deceptive speech through skillful means (*upāya*) should likewise be subject to censure and rejoicing; however, the text is abbreviated.

Furthermore, the causes that constitute deception also pertain to the three poisons: for the sake of seeking fame and profit, falsely proclaiming calamities or blessings, and using clever rhetoric to explain principles in order to protect one's own life and body—these have greed as their cause. To falsely propound heterodox views is merely a desire for...
Harmful intent has hatred as its cause; all other unrealities apart from these two have ignorance as their cause. The conditions are also manifold, namely:
greed, lack, fear, difficulty, resentment from the past, and the factors of the instruments and so forth; the karmic consequences may be understood according to what precedes.
Fourth, the detailed explanation of the characteristics of delusion: these apply to the six consciousnesses and the six objects. Here, we cite the first and the last two.
Because the middle three [categories] are subsumed within it, the text says "up to"; however, if one were to state it in full, it should say "claiming to have heard what was not heard," and so forth.

Since it specifies "regarding the body," how could it refer to only two types of karma? Thus, all such falsehoods are equally grave and differ from the minor offenses categorized separately in the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, since this also pertains to the mind, there is no need to wait for physical action or speech; it refers to that which ought to be performed as prescribed by later regulations.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva constantly gives rise to right speech and right view, and also causes all sentient beings to give rise to right speech and right view.
The commentary explains: "Right speech" is the general category, while "right view" is the specific; that is, seeing what is seen and not seeing what is not seen.
If one were to speak in full detail, it would be from right hearing up to right knowledge; because speech uttered based upon these constitutes the perfection of right speech.
The term "speech" serves as a general heading; here it is merely abbreviated. Regarding "giving birth [to the thought of awakening] and so forth," teaching others to do so is likewise the case.

Because one teaches others to give birth [to that thought], this is precisely the reversal of the two aforementioned delusions regarding self and other. Since a bodhisattva is never otherwise at any time, it is said that they "constantly give birth [to it].
The subsequent section concerns the violation of prohibitions and the resulting offense.
To instead give rise to wrong speech, wrong views, and wrong actions toward all sentient beings constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
The commentary explains:
the phrase "instead" (*er fan*) is used by contrasting others with oneself; alternatively, it means to give rise [to such states] directly toward all sentient beings.
From false speech and so forth, these two potentials are common; "false speech" refers to the function of speech, which becomes entirely perverse simply because the mind within is not upright.

"Listening" and the others are also abbreviated here. As for the path of leading others forward and the gateway of benefiting beings, if one acts like the illusory city (the *gandharva-nagara*), then concealing coarse matters and the like does not constitute an offense.
○ Fifth, the precept against selling intoxicants: After one has become intoxicated, one becomes deluded and frantic, such that there is no evil deed one might not commit;

furthermore, it can facilitate the commission of the previous four [offenses]. This is why it follows them. However, its distinction from the subsequent precept against drinking alcohol lies in the fact that the former harms many people and damages the property of others, whereas the latter merely intoxicates a single person;
thus, their gravity differs. Therefore, the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* states that the sin of selling intoxicants is equal to that of ten oil-pressing wheels.
One brothel is equivalent to ten brothels, etc.; regarding the offense of one tavern, the text has two parts: first, the initial establishment of the precept to cause practice;

second, the subsequent imposition of the offense for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the establishment of what should be ceased; second, the establishment of what should be practiced. Within the first of these, there are again two sections:
first, indicating the characteristics so that they may be known.

"If a Buddha’s disciple personally sells alcohol, teaches others to sell alcohol, or engages in the cause of selling alcohol, the conditions for selling alcohol, the methods of selling alcohol, or the karma of selling alcohol.

The commentary states that this is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the various types of selling alcohol; second, it should be understood that selling alcohol also encompasses the three types of action (body, speech, and mind).
Second, regarding the requisites for selling liquor: due to an excess of greed, with anger and delusion as secondary conditions, one possesses the factors such as yeast, rice, and dregs;
through the skillful means of fermentation, the agent receives payment and provides for their livelihood by giving it to others.
Subsequently, the precept was established to prohibit this.
One must not sell any kind of alcohol, as this gives rise to the causes and conditions for transgression.
The commentary explains that this is divided into two sections: first, citing the actual case to provide the formal prohibition;

second, analyzing the categories according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, which states that there are three types of alcohol—namely, grain-based, fruit-based, and medicinal/alchemical—and further distinguishes between dry, wet, clear, and... [and so forth].
Regarding the second point on turbidity: from a small amount up to as much as a single hair-tip, one must not sell it at all. Second, to reveal the faults and eliminate doubts:
one might ask, "What fault does alcohol have that it should be prohibited entirely? This is why it is said here. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states there are thirty-six faults;
moreover, the ruin of nations, the destruction of families, the loss of one's life, and the failure of governance are mostly caused by alcohol. Thus, one knows the faults of alcohol.
How could such matters be fully recounted? There are thirty-six [instances], which are here explained in brief;
it is because of these profound transgressions that this rule was established. Second, regarding what ought to be done:
a Bodhisattva should give rise to the wisdom of clear penetration toward all sentient beings.
The commentary states: To guide beings according to their faculties with the light of wisdom through the one, three, or five vehicles so that they may attain thorough penetration,
yet subsequently violate prohibitions and commit offenses,
thereby instead giving rise to the deluded minds of all sentient beings— this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

The commentary states: Since one's innate ignorance still requires constant alertness, and even a momentary sleep necessitates exertion to rouse oneself, how could one possibly succumb to greed for wealth or wine, thereby falling into such delusion and madness as to do what ought not be done? Such acts incur guilt.
However, if it is for the benefit of oneself or others, and one seeks to obtain it for that purpose, then it may be sold.
○ Sixth, the explanation of the precepts. The first four are the same as the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*) of the Śrāvakas in the Vinaya;

the latter four are the same as the four grave offenses of the Bodhisattvas in the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Between them, the offense of selling [the Dharma] is added. This is because it is more subtle than selling [alcohol]. Regarding the sequential text, there are two parts:

first, the establishment of the precepts to ensure practice; second, the inflicting of punishment for violating the prohibitions. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the establishment of what ought to be practiced.
Stop! If a son of the Buddha— whether a lay or ordained bodhisattva, a bhikṣu, or a bhikṣuṇī— speaks of the transgressions of others, or teaches others to speak of their transgressions,
including the causes of the transgressions, the conditions for the transgressions, the nature of the transgressions, and the karmic actions of the transgressions.
The commentary is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the categories of those who have committed transgressions, distinguishing between the Great and Small Vehicles;
within the Small Vehicle, there is the distinction between monks and nuns, while within the Great Vehicle, there is the difference between lay and ordained practitioners.

For an ordained Bodhisattva among the monastic community, both the second and first explanations are correct, as they apply to speech and mind, and by extension to the body. The second chapter is likewise. Second, regarding the instruments of transgression, the text is incomplete.

Regarding the explanation of words as the cause for knowing [the truth], it is said that they are connected to the three poisons: because one speaks for the sake of fame, profit, or one's own life, greed is said to be the cause;
because one does not seek to benefit oneself but merely desires to harm others, hatred is said to be the cause;
and apart from these two, all other discourse has delusion as its cause. Furthermore, the conditions (*pratyaya*) are also manifold, namely: wealth, status, power, and former [karmic] connections.
Regarding those dharmas such as evil habitual tendencies and prolixity, one should explain that they are "karmic actions" (karma) in order to make known the skillful means;
this is also taken as the momentum for subsequently establishing what ought to be done.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva hears non-Dharmas spoken within the Buddha-dharma by outsiders, wicked people, or those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), [he should respond accordingly].
The Vinaya constantly gives rise to a compassionate mind to teach and transform these groups of evil people, causing them to give birth to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna.

The commentary states: "Heterodox practitioners (tīrthika) are the 'evil people' outside of the Buddha-dharma; those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are the 'evil people' within the Buddha-dharma.
Because they all lack faith in the Mahāyāna, they are considered evil people; therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* does not permit them to draw near to the Buddha-dharma.
This applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: those who follow external paths (tīrthikas) speak of the faults of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
those of the Hīnayāna speak mostly of the faults of the Mahāyāna, yet also speak of the faults within their own vehicle due to the differences among its various schools.

As for "those who teach," this refers to various skillful means, parables, and modes of expression. "The class of evil persons" refers to the two aforementioned types, while "the good" refers to those who are virtuous.

"Faith" refers to true faith; furthermore, because one who does not believe in the Mahāyāna is not called "virtuous," being able to believe in the One Vehicle Dharma that is difficult to believe constitutes such faith.

Thus, the Mahāyāna of the True Teaching is precisely the One Vehicle. Within this, the details regarding the transformer (the teacher), the transformed (the disciple), self-transformation, and transformation through conditions, as well as the benefits, can be understood by examining them closely. Finally, there is the section on violating prohibitions and the resulting offenses.
If a bodhisattva, on the contrary, speaks of the faults and transgressions within the Buddha-dharma himself, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
The commentary explains: since one ought to even restrain others [from such speech], yet here one speaks of it oneself, it is said that "one conversely speaks of it oneself," and so forth.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states that a renunciant carries a boy in his left hand and a girl in his right hand, going from one tavern to another.
Since he will not pass into parinirvāṇa until the end of this Bhadrakalpa, one should not speak ill of him. However, if one acts as his teacher to instruct those below,
to definitively resolve right from wrong, to earnestly warn others out of loyalty, to suppress the heterodox and manifest the orthodox, to refute the Small Vehicle and manifest the Great,
or if one takes great compassion as the foundation and is solely intent on benefiting others— then there is no fault.

○ Seventh: Praising Oneself and Reviling Others Regarding Violations of the Precepts. This section explains the faults based on what preceded; it follows the sequence of first reviling others and then praising oneself, thereby establishing the order from light to heavy.
Furthermore, this differs from previous instances where self-praise was added. The text has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice;
second, the inflicting of the offense for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, the establishment of that which should be refrained from.

If a disciple of the Buddha praises themselves and disparages others, or likewise teaches others to praise themselves and disparage others—disparaging them by way of cause, condition, dharma, and action.

The commentary explains this in three parts: first, clarifying the categories of praise and disparagement; second, the two types of things; and third, the three karmas, which follow the previous pattern, yet there are three [further aspects].

Regarding the phrases: to praise without disparaging, to disparage without praising, or both to praise and to disparage—furthermore, as will be seen below, merely concealing one's virtues and not mentioning them already constitutes a form of disparagement;
how much more so when one slanders them? Second, concerning the instruments of praise and disparagement:
the text adopts a tactful and compliant approach and is brief regarding self-praise, yet in principle such must exist; the causes also extend to the three poisons, namely, [praising] oneself...
Praising [others] out of greed, or doing so while simultaneously manifesting anger by exposing the faults of others—this very act of disparaging others is precisely anger.

Alternatively, praising [others] while simultaneously manifesting one's own virtues is likewise due to greed. Furthermore, when praise or disparagement is for the sake of fame and profit, greed serves as the cause.
When praise or disparagement is for the sake of causing harm, anger serves as the cause. Beyond these, both praise and disparagement have delusion as their cause. These are the conditions.
The great significance of the Dharma and its practice is the same regarding what ought to be done according to the precepts established both earlier and later;
however, a bodhisattva should instead undergo all the suffering, insults, and evil deeds of all sentient beings upon himself, while giving his own good fortune to others.
The commentary states: To speak excessively is called "defamation" (*nindā*); to cause another to feel shame and embarrassment is "humiliation" (*avamāna*).
It is improper to accept evil offerings while insisting on practicing what is good; subsequently, violating the prohibitions constitutes an offense.
If one proclaims one's own virtues while concealing the good deeds of others, thereby causing those others to suffer defamation, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a Bodhisattva.
The commentary states:
"To foster the evil of others and to boast of one's own skillfulness is something a gentleman (*junzi*) would not do; how much less so for a Bodhisattva?"
Since he has received this censure, his own person has already been tarnished; once he has encountered such solemn disciplinary measures, he ought to incur a heavy penalty.
Nevertheless, regarding the gateway of guidance and encouragement within the teachings, there must be the compassionate skillful means of restraint and concealment.

○ Eighth: The Precept Against Avarice. Regarding the two types of greed [discussed] previously, those concerned with wealth not yet obtained; this present section concerns stinginess regarding wealth already acquired.

The former is coarse while the latter is subtle; this is the sequence of their meaning. The text has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the definition of the offense for violating the prohibition.
Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the establishment of what ought to be refrained from.

"If a disciple of the Buddha is stingy themselves, or teaches others to be stingy—whether through the cause of stinginess, the condition of stinginess, the dharma of stinginess, or the karma of stinginess. Commentary: This passage consists of two sections. The first clarifies the categories of stinginess; the second clarifies the causes and conditions of stinginess, which should be understood as encompassing both the primary and secondary aspects. Furthermore, the causes of stinginess also extend to the three poisons: specifically, the desire to keep for oneself and not give away constitutes the cause of greed (*lobha*). As for the hatred toward others [and thus not giving], it constitutes the cause of anger (*dveṣa*). The cause of ignorance (*moha*) is the failure to understand that giving is a supreme merit. These three poisons constitute the causes of stinginess. As for the conditions of stinginess, they refer to the various external objects that provoke the mind of stinginess. As for the dharma of stinginess, it refers to the teachings of stinginess, such as the false doctrines of the non-Buddhists who claim that giving results in loss and poverty. As for the karma of stinginess, it refers to the physical and verbal actions of withholding wealth and goods from those who seek them. Because one is attached to these things, one does not give to others; this is called the karma of stinginess. Thus, the causes, conditions, dharmas, and karmas of stinginess are fully explained. The commentary explains: "First wealth, then the Dharma. Regarding "a single coin" and so forth, the intent is that even such trifles as a needle or a blade of grass are withheld due to stinginess.
Regarding the phrase "an offense," there are differences between its literal wording and its underlying meaning, as commonly analyzed.

The expression "even as much as a mote of dust" refers to something as minute as a hair-tip, signifying the smallest possible amount; it does not mean that the Dharma-gate possesses the characteristics of dust or hair. These are all instances where the small is used to illustrate the great;
thus, the initial statement "down to" (乃至) does not imply stinginess regarding vast wealth or vast teachings. Subsequently, the conclusion of the transgression establishes the gravity of the offense.
Yet, to instead revile and insult them constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva. The commentary states:

To possess a stinginess that refuses to grant [teachings] cannot be called the mark of great talent. Within the practice of a bodhisattva, how could it be permissible to be parsimonious or secretive regarding wealth and the Dharma?
Not bestowing these upon others is already one transgression; to further revile and insult others on that account warrants the imposition of punishment. If one were to seek further...
If there is something one does not know or cannot understand, or if giving [instruction] would conversely result in harm or obstruct one's own great benefit, then it is not permissible.
However, one must employ skillful means to dismiss them; one must be careful never to revile or insult them, causing them to harbor resentment.

○ Ninth, the Precept Against Anger. Following the aforementioned greed and stinginess, this is the next stage of the dharma of anger. The text has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice;
second, the definition of the offense for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the establishment of that which ought to be ceased.
"If a disciple of the Buddha becomes angry themselves, or teaches others to be angry—whether through the cause of anger, the condition of anger, the dharma of anger, or the karma of anger.

The commentary explains this in two parts: first, the categories of anger; second, the three types of action, which can be understood as follows. Second, regarding the causes that equip anger, these also extend to the three poisons.

This is because competing for fame and profit constitutes the cause of anger, which is rooted in greed (*lobha*). However, when directed toward objects that conflict with one's feelings, it is simply anger (*dveṣa*).
That is the cause. Apart from the favorable and the unfavorable, all instances of hatred have delusion as their cause.

How is it that hatred takes hatred as its cause? Because the seeds and the manifest [states] are distinct. As for the conditions, these are designated as objects such as those who are beneficial or harmful, enemies, and so forth;
they refer to the performance of preparatory actions, the manifestation of anger and malice, and likewise take these as their objective basis. Second, they are what ought to be restrained.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva should give rise to roots of goodness in all sentient beings and engage in matters free from contention, constantly generating a mind of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*).

The commentary explains: "roots of goodness" refers to non-anger; "matters free from contention" refers to the karma arising from the root of goodness that is non-anger, namely, being humble, gentle, patient, and skillfully reconciling disputes. "Loving-kindness and compassion" means not merely being free from anger.
Furthermore, one who is able to uproot suffering not only through non-contention (*araṇā*) but also by bestowing happiness—such a practitioner is called filial and obedient.

Conversely, to commit an offense by violating prohibitions and instead reviling all sentient beings, even down to those that are not sentient beings, with harsh speech; [this is the second violation].

If, after being struck with the hand or beaten with knives and staves, one’s anger still does not cease, and even when the other person seeks reconciliation with kind words and offers a sincere apology,
one remains resentful and cannot let go of the anger— this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
The commentary states: Not all sentient beings are exclusively human;
those who are not sentient beings include insentient objects, such as when one falls down and curses the earth. Even with such evil speech, the three lower karmas are fully present.
Yet, conversely, there are six layers of matters that accord with compassion rather than non-compassion: first, excessive anger; second, verbal abuse; and so forth.
Third, striking with the hand; fourth, using both [hand and foot]; fifth, employing knives and staves; sixth, performing prostrations of repentance without understanding [the offense].

Because such transgressions are repeated, it is said that one "instead acts perversely. However, if one acts out of compassion for the benefit of sentient beings—as in the cases of Ta-ha (Dharmarakṣita) and Devadatta—there is no offense.
○ Tenth: The Precept Against Slandering. Since this [precept] follows immediately upon the precept against anger, it is because this is a false view;

therefore, next, regarding anger, it is because this can cause the Three Jewels to be severed. Next is the explanation of the text of the regulation, which has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the inflicting of punishment for violating the prohibition.
Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the establishment of what should be refrained from.

"If a Buddha’s disciple slanders the Triple Gem themselves, or teaches others to slander the Triple Gem—whether through the causes of slander, the conditions of slander, the dharma of slander, or the karma of slander.

The commentary divides this into two parts; first, it clarifies the types of slander. If a person says that the Tathāgata is definitively great, definitively small, definitively existent, definitively empty, definitively one, definitively many, definitively so, or definitively otherwise—all such claims constitute slandering the Buddha. If one does not understand the four intentions (*abhiprāya*)... To disparage the *siddhāntas* and the three [vehicles], and so forth, is to slander the Dharma. If one does not understand the provisional and the real, the inverse and the compliant, or the internal and external matters and principles—these being the skillful means—it is to slander the Sangha.
Thus, the Buddha encompasses both the True and the Responsive; the Dharma includes both the Half and the Full; and the Sangha comprises both the Holy and the Ordinary.
These three categories can be understood through the three karmas. Hereafter, the causes for such slandering will be clarified, which likewise apply to all three.
Regarding "poison": if one slanders out of devotion to wealth and status or to accommodate flatterers, greed (*lobha*) is the cause;
if one slanders out of enmity or resentment, hatred (*dveṣa*) is the cause; if one slanders due to lack of understanding, lack of faith, or through mere spontaneity, delusion (*moha*) is the cause.
Regarding "conditions": these include one's own position and rank—both those already attained and those not yet attained—as well as resentment toward others and false teachers.

Heterodox teachings, frivolous discourse, and the like are "dharmas"; skillfully explaining principles is "action"; manifesting those practices or making them one's primary pursuit is "what is to be done," which was later codified as a duty.
Yet when a Bodhisattva hears even a single word of slander against the Buddha from a non-Buddhist or an evil person, that sound is as painful as three hundred spears piercing him.
"Piercing the heart.

The commentary explains: "Heterodox practitioners" (*tīrthika*) refers to those who hold wrong views and lack faith; "evil persons" refers to those who slander out of greed, hatred, and so forth, and who are not necessarily devoid of faith.
Heterodox practitioners are not non-evil persons, but because their transgressions are particularly grave, they are so designated.
Regarding those who slander the Buddha with biased words, there are briefly two points: first, that certain phrases are inconvenient; second, that the root encompasses the branches.
Thus, the Dharma is what was spoken by the Buddha, and the Saṃgha consists of the Buddha’s disciples.
As for the word *gō* (spear), it refers to a class of weapons such as halberds. Although the slanders are few, the piercing spears are many; they pierce the heart and cause deep regret.

The reason this is so extreme is that Bodhisattvas burn their bodies as offerings to the Buddha, sacrifice their lives to seek the Dharma, and endure suffering to save sentient beings, all for the sake of perpetuating the Triple Gem;
yet now, conversely, one sees the severance of the Triple Gem—how could this not be painful?
Second, violating prohibitions constitutes an offense.
How much more so if one personally slanders [the Dharma] without generating faith or a heart of filial obedience, yet instead assists evil people and those with wrong views in their slander—
this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
The commentary states: Seeing others slandering [the Triple Gem] and feeling no pain is already a transgression; to then slander them oneself is even worse—hence the word "how much more so" (*jue*).
Furthermore, seeing others slander and not stopping it is itself one fault; to then assist them is even more so—hence the phrase "on the contrary, they do not give rise to faith.

Thus, failing to give rise to faith is the same as being a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*), and failing to give rise to a mind of filial piety is the same as being an evil person. Since they slander the Triple Gem, [the fault is grave].
To fail to accord with the principle and Dharma of the Three Jewels is to fail in the way of the Ultimate Path; to fail in this is likewise unfilial.

Because such failure harms sentient beings, it is also unfilial toward one's parents. However, if one were to destroy the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) while exalting the Greater Vehicle (Mahāyāna), or discard the provisional while advancing the real, the gate of "suppression and exaltation" would be entirely abandoned.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "I observe those of the Lesser Vehicle as being like those who are blind."
This is precisely of that category; one must rely on principle and not indulge sentiment. Following this, there is the conclusion of the exhortation and the pointing to the extensive text.

Because there is no pure precept, it does not depend on physical form or clothing; the above applies generally to both ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), while from here on, it refers exclusively to the Mahāyāna.

Among the four stages of "setting out" (*prasthāna*) and so forth, these are the causes; within these, there are differences between those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and those who have entered the stages, as well as between the noble ones (*ārya*) and others.

The latter two are both results. That which is eternally abiding is the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, which reveals that its essence is identical to the cause; therefore, it is called "Buddha-nature. This is clarified by this [passage].
Regarding "permanently abiding and permanent": this refers to the wondrous fruit of *nirvāṇa*, which is the locus of the wondrous practice of *bodhi*.
Because it accomplishes the adornment of myriad virtues, it is so called. Alternatively, "Buddha-nature" is *nirvāṇa* and "permanently abiding";

these terms apply to both fruits, as both fruits are permanently abiding. Alternatively, Buddha-nature is that which is attained as the fruit; Buddha-nature is permanently abiding, and the wondrous fruit is [the same].
"Because of [clinging to] nirvana and bodhi, everything is lost" concludes the preceding discussion on the causes and effects of both the ordinary/small vehicles and the Mahāyāna;

alternatively, it may mean that all wholesome qualities—whether tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*)—are entirely lost. This is followed by the explanation of falling into the three evil realms.
Falling into the three evil realms, for two or three kalpas they do not hear the names of their parents or the Three Jewels.
The commentary explains that "two, three, etc. refers to the gravity of the offense committed within the evil states and the degree of prior wholesome roots;

thus, one may pass through two or three kalpas within a single [offense], or pass through two or three kalpas collectively across two or three [offenses], according to the nature of the transgression.
The degrees of gravity likewise apply to all three categories: small, medium, and great. As for those who have not even heard the names of their parents:

they are born by transformation in hell; as ghosts, they are mostly so; and though they may be among animals, because they possess much ignorance, they do not know [their parents], yet this is no different from having none at all.
Regarding the Triple Gem, it is certainly appropriate that they should never hear its name in such difficult circumstances; otherwise, one would subsequently be bound by what ought not to be.
For this reason, one should not commit each [offense] individually.
The commentary states: Since the retribution is such as this, the principle must be firm and certain; like a form carrying its shadow, one can never escape it.

From here on, the second section clarifies that the essence of these minor defilement precepts is not a grave transgression; they are termed "light" because they defile and pollute pure conduct.

The myriad vastnesses are as numerous as dust motes; although they have been briefly indicated here, one may reflect upon them through three pairs [of verses].

these shall be shown in the text as it unfolds. The text has three parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing what follows; second, the formal recitation of the characteristics of the precepts; third, the conclusion with an exhortation to practice and study. Now...
First: The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying, "The ten *pātimokkha* rules have already been expounded; now the forty-eight minor precepts shall be explained."
The explanation may be understood as follows. Next, the formal recitation of the text on the characteristics of the precepts consists of five sections:

and (5) clarifying the nine precepts concerning receiving the precepts and so forth. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, fully manifesting the characteristics of the precepts; second, the conclusion.
