○ First, regarding the precept against treating one's teachers and elders with contempt: since one has newly received the precepts, one must follow the instructions of the teacher;

conversely, to give rise to contempt results in the loss of instruction and the deficiency of practice, and thus this rule was established first. The text has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its observance; second, the prohibition against violating it.
Regarding the section on the establishment of the offense, there are two parts. First, it instructs on complying with and upholding the precepts.

The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, when one wishes to receive the position of a king, or the position of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), or when ministers and officials receive their positions, one should first receive the Bodhisattva Precepts.
Then all ghosts and spirits will protect the person of the king and the persons of the ministers and officials."
The Buddha rejoiced.
The commentary explains that the first section clarifies the station [of the recipient], causing them to receive the rank of a king as previously described;

the second section reveals the benefit and removes doubt. The doubt is as follows: "Does one receive the position but not the precepts? or "Does one receive the precepts but not the position? [The text] clarifies both.
What is the loss? Therefore, it is said next: "Because one possesses the precepts, one accords with the will of the sages above and thus gains the joy of all Buddhas;
below, one harmonizes with the multitude of spirits and thus gains the protection of ghosts and deities. When there is a calamity, they immediately provide protection; otherwise, this is not so.
Thus, there would be no means to preserve the state and govern the people. Afterwards, this leads to spiritual resonance.
Regarding the practice of honoring and supporting them: once you have received the precepts, you should give rise to a mind of filial piety and a mind of reverence.

Upon seeing elders, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), instructors (*ācārya*), fellow students, those of the same views, or those who practice together, you should rise to welcome them, prostrate, and inquire after their well-being.
The commentary states: "Filial and obedient" refers to being moved by their kindness; "reverent" refers to admiring their virtue. "Elder" (*sthavira*) means the most honored among the assembly.
"Preceptor" (*upādhyāya*)—translated here as "near-reading"—refers to one from whom one personally receives service and the transmission of the sutras and Dharma.

"Ācārya"—translated here as "model"—is so called because they instruct others with this [conduct] to bring them to accomplishment. Regarding the two aforementioned [categories], one properly receives these [teachings] alone.

Regarding the precepts: because one must show respect to all others without exception, those who are senior among fellow students—whether they are superior in years or virtue, or equal in views and practice—are of two types who may not necessarily have been one's teacher;
toward them, one must certainly give rise to a humble mind. Whether this relationship is general or specific, if it is specific, one must treat them as superior and serve them.

If someone comes from outside, one should immediately go out to welcome them and provide lodging; once they have departed, one should pay them respects. If there is anything that seems improper, one should inquire about it;

even if there is nothing that causes discomfort, one must still offer a greeting. When a visitor sees that one has come from afar, one should promptly rise to welcome them, receiving them with prostrations and inquiries after their well-being.
Later, to violate these prohibitions constitutes an offense.
Yet, if a Bodhisattva instead gives rise to arrogance, pride, delusion, or anger, failing to rise to welcome him,

prostrate, inquire after his well-being, or provide every kind of Dharma-conforming offering— whether by selling oneself, one's kingdom, city, sons, daughters, or the seven treasures and various goods to provide for him—
if one does not do so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

The commentary explains that the first section of the three parts clearly elucidates the transgressions. Attachment to one’s own prosperity is called *māna* (pride); relying on oneself to despise others is called *abhimāna* (arrogance).
Delusion (*moha*) is the cause of these two, while hatred (*dveṣa*) is their result. Furthermore, failing to give rise to [virtues] toward those below can also be termed a cause.
Thus, pride and arrogance are the opposites of the aforementioned respect, and hatred and delusion are the reversals of the aforementioned filial piety.
The above are all states of mind that are contrary [to the Dharma]. Each statement contains two meanings;

that is to say, regarding each instance of a teacher or each matter of making offerings, there are three ways of offering according to the Dharma: first, offering through reverence, such as welcoming and prostrating;
second, offering through material things, such as incense and flowers; and third, offering through practice, which means practicing according to the teachings. Furthermore—
This is called "Dharma-offering" (*dharmapūjā*). It primarily clarifies the first two types [of offerings], while implicitly including the subsequent practices;

this can be understood by reversing the previous explanation. Second, it specifically demonstrates the removal of doubts. Someone might ask: "Veneration and respect are performed by all people according to the occasion, yet there are inequalities in wealth and poverty.

How, then, can one perform offerings? This is why the text speaks of selling oneself, as well as one's sons and daughters—this refers to those who are poor. As for "the body," it refers to the physical person.

These [treasures] apply universally to both monastics and laity, as well as to men and women; however, they pertain only to the laity, who may manifest them with great solemnity. It is not necessarily the case that one must be destitute of a kingdom or a city; rather, it refers specifically to those who are householders.
Furthermore, what is called a "kingdom" (rāṣṭra) is that which is governed by commoners, while what is called a "city" (nagara) is that which serves as their seat of authority.

These [treasures] apply to all four wheels (*cakra*) and include both the grain and the ruinous [treasures]. Regarding the seven treasures (*saptaratna*), there are two types: first, those that apply exclusively to a Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*), namely the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) and the elephant-treasure (*hastiratna*).
The phrase "the two [types] of equal" refers to minor kings; the phrase "various items such as gold and silver" also has two meanings: that which is offered and that which is sold.
"That which is offered" refers to whatever is required by the recipient, while "that which is sold" refers to whatever one personally possesses.

These apply universally to all great numbers. When speaking of "a hundred" in relation to a superior, it refers to making an offering; this refers to those who are senior fellow students (*mahāśramaṇa*) and above.

Furthermore, if one is ill and unable to rise or inquire after others, or if one is poor and cannot provide for one's own body, and there is no one to purchase [the goods], one should not give rise to pride.

Regarding the formulation of the offense, there are two parts: first, a general indication based on the matter; second, specific regulations based on the person. This is the first part.

if one passes a vessel of alcohol with one's own hand to give someone else to drink, one shall be without hands for five hundred lifetimes, let alone drinking it oneself.

"If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally eats meat"—this can be understood from the subsequent text which establishes the prohibition by explaining the loss of benefit for others.
"No meat whatsoever may be eaten. Indeed, those who eat meat sever the seeds of the nature of great compassion within all sentient beings.
Upon seeing [the meat], they arise and depart.

The commentary divides this into two parts: first, the statement "all that is to be abandoned" indicates that all such things are included within meat; second, it demonstrates the faults [of eating it], stating that it severs great compassion and so forth.
Regarding internal faults, it refers to the cause for transformation; when habitual practice becomes one's nature, it stands in opposition to the nature of manifest activity.

This refers to the seeds or natures that are formed through the perfuming of active manifestations (*samudācāra*). Consequently, all those of inferior capacity or externalists lose their connection with the transformative conditions (*pariṇāmanā-ālambana*).
Some say that because animals see blood-light upon the heads of those who eat meat, they become terrified and abandon them;
this is why the boy practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*) contended with the geese over the path, and the bhikṣu carrying a bird for slaughter caused a divergence in the [narrative] branches.
This clarifies the loss of one's own benefit in order to effect its cessation.
Therefore, no Bodhisattva may eat the flesh of any sentient being; to eat meat incurs immeasurable sin.

The commentary is divided into two parts. First, the designation of what is to be abandoned: the term "therefore" refers back to the preceding text. Second, the demonstration of its transgression as a condition for killing:
it is said that one incurs immeasurable sin, as stated in a verse from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*: "Meat does not arise spontaneously; it is all obtained by taking life.
If a person does not refrain from meat, they are all like thieves who rob others of their lives. This contradicts [the opponent's position] later on.
This prohibits the commission of offenses.
If one intentionally consumes [meat], one commits a minor offense of defilement (*āpatti-dukkaṭa*).

The commentary states: "If, for the sake of converting beings through shared activity—as in the case of Master Zhigong and others—one is already not attached to the flavor of meat and lacks [the desire for it]..."
What is injured here constitutes no offense; all else is impermissible.

○ Fourth, the precept against consuming pungent herbs and impurities. Having previously discussed the consumption of blood and flesh while they still possess life, this present rule concerns the consumption of pungent herbs once their life has ceased;
it follows as the next item. The text is divided into two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice.
If a Buddha’s disciple does not eat the five pungent roots— garlic, leeks, scallions, onions, and asafoetida—
these five kinds may not be eaten among any types of food whatsoever.
The commentary states: The first section provides a general classification by citing the five types of foul-smelling, pungent herbs known as the "five pungents" (*pañca-garaka*).
The second section lists their names and provides specific prohibitions: *laśuna* (garlic) is as commonly seen; *gṛñjana* refers to mountain *gṛñjana*;

it exists in the northern regions but not in the south of the Yangtze River; *kārilla* refers to wild *gṛñjana*, while *laśuna* is the domestic variety; and regarding *hiṅgu* (asafoetida), there are various explanations.
*Yun tai* (mustard) has leaves resembling wild garlic (*yèsuàn*) and roots and stems resembling leeks;
it is also called *wúláo zǐ*. It is abundant in the regions south of the Yangtze River but is not found in the northern lands.

Some say this is the Sanskrit name for *āśvaghana* (asafoetida), yet other sources list *zhìfēi*, *cǎo*, *xīng*, and garlic as the five pungent vegetables (*wǔxīn*), which differs from this [identification]. Thirdly, regarding food, it is universally prohibited for all.
The phrase "speaking with force" refers to the five pungent roots and various foods; if one subsequently violates the prohibitions, one incurs an offense.
If one intentionally consumes them, one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
The commentary states: "One should dwell in fragrance and purity, yet instead one perfumes oneself with filth and offends the worthy and holy; therefore, one deserves this punishment."
If it is for the purpose of curing illness or for a great benefit, one should immediately grant permission; otherwise, it is absolutely not permitted. ○ Fifth:
The precept against concealing [a fault] while not being a co-resident. The former [precept] was for self-purification, whereas this is for purifying others.
Furthermore, the former concerned the defilement of objects, while this concerns the defilement of conduct. The text has two parts: first, the formulation of the precept to ensure its practice.

If a Buddha’s disciple sees any sentient beings who have violated the eight precepts, the five precepts, or the ten precepts; who have breached the prohibitions, committed the seven heinous offenses, or fallen into the eight difficulties;
or who have committed any other transgressions against the precepts, they should instruct them in repentance.

The commentary is divided into two parts. First, it identifies the sentient beings who are the objects of the precepts as those capable of transgression, while all others are merely objects of violation.

Regarding the eight precepts and the five precepts: the "five" refers to the first five of the eight; "sexual misconduct" is restricted to improper conduct. The "ten precepts" refer to the śrāmaṇera precepts.
"Violating prohibitions" refers to the mahābhikṣu precepts and the bodhisattva precepts. The "seven heinous offenses" (ānantarya) are those that involve shedding the blood of a Buddha.
Blood and so forth are as explained in the following text. Regarding the "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), these refer to those such as the blind and the deaf;

here, we take their causes—that is, the persons who create the causes for the eight difficulties. "All below" serves to conclude the preceding discourse. Alternatively, it may refer to the remaining two [difficulties].
"Virtuous conduct" (*śīlacaryā*)—in Sanskrit *kṣamā*, which here means "repentance"—refers to seeing that there has been some deficiency or transgression, and requiring that one reform.
This present text is a combination of both Chinese and Sanskrit traditions; hereafter, to violate the prohibitions constitutes an offense.

If a Bodhisattva does not instruct [the offender] to repent, nor does he dwell with them, share the same monastic provisions, participate in the *poṣadha* together with the community, or recite the precepts as one assembly, yet fails to bring forth their offense and instruct them to reform, he commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
The commentary states: "Living together" means sharing the same dwelling place; "sharing benefits" means sharing the same profit, which also implies sharing the same food;
"performing the *poṣadha* together" means sharing the same Dharma. The term is correctly called *poṣadha*, which here is translated as "pure abiding.

As for the aforementioned faults and transgressions, there are four grades in detail. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, light transgressions are subject to reprimand, medium transgressions to punishment, and grave transgressions to expulsion.

If you have committed an offense and, when it is pointed out, do not repent or submit, and others depart while you remain—or if you yourself depart—nevertheless, if you continue to dwell together with them, you commit an offense. Sixth:
The Precept Against Failing to Request the Dharma. Previously, one failed to respect those who had lost [their status]; here, one fails to respect those who possess virtue.

Regarding the subsequent text concerning seeking [the precepts], there are two parts: first, the formulation of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the establishment of the offense for violating the prohibition.
Within the first part, there are two sections: first, citing the circumstances of the precept; second, manifesting the practice of the precept. This is the first [section].

If a disciple of the Buddha sees a Mahāyāna Dharma Master, a fellow student of the Mahāyāna, or one who shares the same views and practices, coming to enter a monastery, a private residence, a city, or a town—
from a distance of a hundred li, a thousand li, or even further— then [he should act as follows].

The commentary states: A "Mahāyāna Dharma Master" is so called because they realize the principles of the Mahāyāna, practice the conduct of the Mahāyāna, aspire toward the fruit of the Mahāyāna, and preach the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
Because fellow students study under the same teacher, they share the same views and the same conduct; however, it is not necessarily the case that they must have studied under the same master.
This designation applies specifically to those who adhere to the Mahāyāna and does not permit one to associate with those who study the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna.

Therefore, the phoenix and peacock do not respond to the presence of crows and magpies; likewise, monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) are designated for renunciant bodhisattvas, while houses and cities are designated for lay bodhisattvas.
However, houses encompass both the noble and the humble, whereas cities are restricted solely to kings and lords.

If one considers the places where they encounter [others], this distinction may also be applied broadly. As for the phrase "a hundred li," the intent clarifies that it refers to those who are on the road.

There is no need to go far to welcome [the Dharma Master], for his conduct shall subsequently manifest the precepts. This section has two parts. First, regarding the command to provide respectful support without deficiency:
one must rise to welcome him upon arrival and see him off upon departure; perform prostrations and make offerings;

provide daily sustenance at the three times of day, consisting of three *liang* of gold worth of food of a hundred flavors, as well as beds, seats, and medicine; and attend to the Dharma Master with all necessary provisions, providing everything he requires.

[The text] says: "The commentary is divided into two parts. First, regarding the explanation of the rituals for respectful service, such as welcoming and seeing off, this means: rising to welcome those who arrive, performing prostrations and making offerings;
seeing off those who depart by making offerings, performing prostrations, and escorting them; and the three times of offering, which refers to the morning..."
Because one provides medicinal decoctions and other necessities during the middle watch of the night, this second point clarifies what is esteemed in making offerings. Regarding "two pieces of gold":

since the gate of the Buddha’s teaching delivers one from the suffering of the three realms, its kindness exceeds that which is boundless; how then could it be limited to three pieces of gold? Regarding "hundred-flavored foods and so forth":

this means offering food at the time of the *zhāi* (fasting/observance) and presenting drinks at other times; providing a bed for reclining and resting, spreading out a seat for preaching the Dharma, and so on.

When they were unwell, he provided them with medicine; when they had needs, he granted them what was required. Thus it is said that he attended to all matters. Afterwards, he requested the Dharma without weariness.

He constantly invited Dharma masters to preach the Dharma at the three times of the day, and every day at those three times he performed prostrations, never giving rise to anger, resentment, or affliction.
With a mind [intent on] the Dharma, one requests the Dharma even at the cost of sacrificing one's body, never flagging in effort.

The commentary explains that requesting the Dharma consists of verbal activity (vocal karma), prostration consists of physical activity (bodily karma), and non-anger and so forth consist of mental activity (mental karma).
This means that one does not become angry or distressed because the Dharma contradicts one’s own inclinations; nor does one fail to inquire or fail to speak. Rather, one speaks much without anger.

Not being provoked is the opposite of this; it can also be described as "dual," meaning that one does not feel anger when spoken to in ways that contradict one's feelings, nor does one feel resentment when spoken of in profound matters that one does not understand.
For those who would sacrifice their bodies for the sake of the Dharma, their lives have been spent in vain through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

To lose one’s body for the sake of the Dharma—how could this be contrary to principle? The "Snow Mountain Youth" (Śvetaketu) and others are prime examples of this. Hereafter, [the text discusses] contrariety...
This constitutes a transgression of the prohibitions. If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
The commentary states: "If there is truly no anger or malice, but [the person] is unable to act due to illness, or is unable to provide offerings due to poverty, or is deaf or mute..."
If one is unable to resolve difficult points because others are not equal to oneself, there is no offense provided one does not request or inquire about them.

○ Seventh, regarding listening to the lecture hall with a distracted mind: before the precept, one encounters someone who does not request [the teaching]; this clarifies that one does not listen when there is a lecture.

The text has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the definition of the offense for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sections. First:
He points out the place where the lectures are held:
"If a disciple of the Buddha sees that there is a place for preaching the Dharma, Vinaya, Sutras, and Shastras in any location, or within a great house where the Dharma is being preached."
The commentary states: *Vinaya* is translated here as "extinction" (*miè*). It is so called because it extinguishes karma and extinguishes afflictions, leading to the extinction of their fruits.

As for *lü* (vinaya), it means "dharma," in the sense of a rule or standard; since "dharma" encompasses the *Abhidharma*, the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) are thereby complete. Later, an imperial decree was issued ordering that it be permitted to study and receive [this teaching].
A newly initiated bodhisattva should carry the scrolls of the sūtras and vinaya to the place where the Dharma master resides to listen, receive, and inquire about them;
they should likewise go to all places where the Dharma is preached, whether in mountain forests, beneath trees, in monastic quarters, or elsewhere, to listen and receive the teachings.

The commentary states: Regarding the "volumes of Sūtra and Vinaya," these may be either commentaries (*śāstra*) or the original texts (*mūla*). Those who listen and receive them do so to hear the words and to practice their meaning.
Those who inquire may be either ignorant or doubtful; thus, elucidating the fundamental principles benefits all disciples.

"In mountain forests or under trees" refers to the aforementioned "everywhere"; "monastic dwellings" (*saṃghārāma*) refers to the aforementioned "houses"; alternatively, "houses" may refer to mountains.

The phrase "monastic dwellings in the forests" refers specifically to those locations, while the subsequent mention of "all such places" constitutes the general category. How could the sites for expounding the Dharma be restricted to these three alone?
To subsequently violate this prohibition constitutes an offense.
If one fails to go there to listen, receive instruction, or inquire about the teachings, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

The commentary states: It is only logical that a newly initiated bodhisattva should act in this manner; if they lack what has been heard, it will be difficult for them to practice through understanding and application.
Even if one must risk their extraordinary life and limb, they ought to seek out [the teaching]; to have a lecture given and not listen—how could such a failure be more grievous?
If the world were already nineteen years old and fire were emerging from within the water, how could it be saved? Unless there is some other great benefit, or perhaps an illness...
If obstacles prevent success, or if the other party is not equal to oneself, one may refrain from going without committing an offense.

○ Eighth: The Precept Against Turning Away from the Right and Following the Wrong. Although one has diligently studied the Dharma previously, one must recognize that a deviation of even a hair’s breadth between the wrong and the right brings calamity for ten thousand kalpas; therefore, this must be distinguished next.

If a disciple of the Buddha, with a mind that rejects the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas of the eternal Dharma, declares them not to be the words of the Buddha, yet instead accepts and upholds the precepts of the two vehicles—
the śrāvakas— and the evil views of external paths, as well as all their prohibitions, heterodox views, sūtras, and vinayas, they commit a secondary offense of defilement.
The commentary states: "Permanently abiding" refers to the wondrous principle elucidated by the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya;

"permanently abiding sūtras and vinaya" is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound, for that which is elucidated is the primary referent. To say "it was not spoken by the Buddha" means that one's emotions have been stirred within and manifested in speech;
thus, it is known that both the karma of speech and the karma of mind constitute acts of rebellion. As for the "Two Vehicles," this refers to the Second Vehicle.
This refers to the Pratyekabuddhas; otherwise, how would they differ from the Śrāvakas? To speak of them, it is simply that their objects of contemplation—the Truths—are different.
As for the "non-Buddhists" (tīrthikas), these are those whose paths lie outside the Buddha-dharma. "Holders of evil views" refers to those who do not believe in the emptiness of phenomena;

these include the two vehicles who deny cause and effect through their evil views, as well as non-Buddhists who hold evil views. Regarding "all prohibitive precepts," [the gravity of] killing is considered more serious than stealing.
Reaching five *māṣaka* coins does not obstruct [the path]; mental transgressions are of great benefit, yet there is no allowance for delusion regarding great compassion and so forth.
The prohibitions of the two vehicles concern crows, chickens, deer, dogs, and the like; these are the prohibitions of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Those who hold false views regarding the *sūtras* and *vinaya* rely on the "half-letters" (*ardhakṣara*) and the "Great Existence" (*mahāsattva*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* states: even if a bodhisattva were to [commit offenses] equal in number to the sands of the Ganges...

If one experiences the five sublime sensual pleasures for an eon, it is not called a violation of the precepts; however, if even a single thought of the mind of the Two Vehicles arises, it is called a violation.
Furthermore, the text below states that if one wishes to subdue others, one must be well-versed in their own schools;
provided one does not turn away from or slander the Mahāyāna Dharma, there is no offense in accepting those [teachings].

○ Ninth: The Precept Against Seeing Sickness and Not Providing Aid. This follows the preceding wisdom; it is the practice of a Bodhisattva characterized by compassion. The text is divided into two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice;
second, the definition of the offense for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, a universal exhortation based on principle.
If a disciple of the Buddha sees anyone who is ill, they should always provide for them with offerings no different from those given to the Buddha himself.
Among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit consisting of caring for the sick is the foremost.

The commentary explains these two sections as follows: First, it raises the supreme and correct exhortation that one should honor and provide for those who care for the sick with a mind identical to that of a Buddha;
thus, both the object of the offering and the subject who offers are like the Buddha. Second, it reveals the merit [of this act] to sever doubts. Someone might ask:
"Why are both the mental state and the object of the practice like the Buddha? And why do you urge me to perform this practice? It is for this reason that the following is said.
Regarding the eight fields of merit, one tradition states: first, a fine well by a desolate road; second, bridges over waterways; third, leveling dangerous passes;
fourth, filial piety toward one's parents; fifth, making offerings to śramaṇas; sixth, attending to the sick;

seventh, rescuing those in peril and distress; eighth, establishing an unrestricted assembly (amogha-pūjā). Another tradition states that the Three Jewels constitute three [fields], followed by one's father.

The mother, the teacher-monk (śramaṇī), those who are impoverished, those who are ill, and animals—these eight objects are all capable of generating merit, and are therefore called "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Regarding the term "foremost," since the Buddha occupies the first position, the text states that he is no different from the Buddha;
for this reason, he alone is specifically exhorted. Second, there is the specific exhortation based on kinship.

If one’s parents, teachers, monastics, or disciples suffer from diseases, impaired faculties, or the afflictions of the hundred kinds of illness, one should provide for them all so that they may recover.
The commentary states:
"Parents, teachers, and monastics" refers to both worldly and transworldly parents, as well as the physical body and the Dharma-body.
Because all possess the grace of the Great Heaven, disciples are able to succeed to the Three Jewels;

although this applies to all things, these three are particularly urgent, and thus they are specifically exhorted. The hundredfold teachings encompass all principles; to save all who suffer is what is called "Great Compassion.
Hereafter, violating prohibitions shall result in the incurrence of guilt.
If a Bodhisattva, out of an evil mind, a mind of anger, or a mind of resentment, fails to look after others— even within monasteries, cities, towns, wildernesses,
mountain forests, or on roads— and does not provide relief to those who are sick, they commit a minor offense.
The commentary states: An evil mind is that which finds fault with the matter of illness. A mind of hatred (*dveṣa*) is that in which compassion does not arise.

A mind of resentment (*upanāha*) is that which possesses long-standing enmity; or, because of resentment, the desire for a person to die quickly is called a mind of hatred, while the desire for them to remain ill is called a mind of resentment.
Thus, resentment serves as the general category, while hatred and evil are its specific instances. Furthermore, there is also envy (*īrṣyā*).
For these reasons, one may encounter hostility due to manifest malice, anger due to past grudges, or resentment. A "monastery" refers to the place where teachers, monks, and disciples are ill;

a "city" refers to the place where parents and relatives are ill; and "mountains, forests, and so forth" refers generally to places where all people are ill—these may overlap and need not be restricted to specific locations.
Nevertheless, the Bodhisattva takes compassion as his heart and the salvation of beings as his practice.

For this reason, when the girl Candrottarā cut off her breasts to save the mother of the laywoman Viśākhā, and when [the Buddha] cut flesh from his thigh to nourish a sick monk, he did so out of patience toward his father, the King; likewise, he wounded his own flesh to cure a disease.
Therefore, if one does not act otherwise, one commits this offense. If, however, one truly possesses no mind of anger or resentment, but is merely obstructed by the difficulty of illness, or...
If there is benefit exceeding this or that, or if one lacks nothing oneself, then it is not so, and there is no offense.

○ Tenth: The Precept Against Possessing Various Unlawful Items. Previously, there was no intention to rescue things; this possession of instruments for harming living beings belongs to the category of evil.
The text has two parts: first, the formulation of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the definition of the offense for violating the prohibition. Regarding the former:
Second, first citing the specific instances to provide a formal prohibition:

"If you, O Sons of the Buddha, must not keep any swords, staves, bows, arrows, spears, axes, or implements for combat and war, nor any evil nets, snares, or traps that are instruments for killing living beings; none of these may be kept."
The commentary states: "Weapons of combat" refers to swords, staves, and so forth, which are instruments for killing; "nets and snares" refers to those used for trapping.
The term "instruments of killing" encompasses both the language of weapons of combat and the specific category of traps.

Regarding the phrase "all such things," since there are many varieties within each of the two aforementioned categories, they are collectively regulated by terms such as crossbows, traps, nets, and so forth. Subsequently...
This is a solemn admonition regarding skillful means:
even if a Bodhisattva were to have their own parents killed, they would not seek retribution; how much less so for killing any other sentient being?

The commentary states: Since one does not repay even great enmity toward one's parents, how could it be appropriate to inflict injury or harm upon others who have committed no fault? How could such violence be justified?

If one knows that keeping these [weapons] is indeed contrary to the Dharma, yet later violates the prohibition and incurs an offense, or if one intentionally keeps knives and staves, one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*). The commentary states:

if one temporarily uses these as a means of authority for the sake of protecting the Triple Gem, one's parents, and so forth, provided there is ultimately no intent to kill, then [there is no offense].
Regarding items such as swords and staves, or tools for setting nets and traps, there is no allowance for their possession; this will be explained in detail later in the concluding exhortation.
Thus, these ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind; they shall be elucidated extensively in the following six chapters.
The commentary is self-evident.

From here below, the second section clarifies the ten precepts for entering an army and so forth; this text consists of two parts as per the previous model, wherein the ten precepts within the first part are divided into ten sections.

○ First, regarding the precept on entering the army through a pass and previously possessing weapons of war: this is for the purpose of serving as a messenger in battle, and the categories of meaning follow one another.

The text has two parts: first, the formal enactment of the precept to be observed; second, the definition of the offense for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the formal enactment based on the specific matter.

The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, for the sake of profit or out of an evil mind, you must not serve as a messenger between nations, nor join military arrays, nor lead armies into battle to slaughter immeasurable sentient beings."
The commentary states: "Gain and offerings" refers to wealth and status; "evil intent" refers to harboring resentment from past enmities;

and "envoys for a state" and so forth refers to matters such as plotting military arrays, like those of Luan Bu and others. As for "killing immeasurable sentient beings," it refers to matters such as those at burial mounds and the like.
This constitutes a simultaneous violation of the precept against killing; however, because the matter of one's life is considered minor, it is treated as a gateway [to other offenses]. (2)
Using the light case to illustrate the heavy:
if even a bodhisattva is not permitted to enter an army and move about within it, how much less so for one who intentionally acts as a traitor to the state?
The commentary states: "If movement for no purpose is already forbidden because it stems from a life of evil intent, how could one possibly tolerate such a person?"
This constitutes an offense against the prohibitions.
If one acts intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light stain).
The commentary states: If it is for the sake of a good heart and not for the sake of profit or sustenance, and one wishes to bring about peace and harmony, then one may go.

○ Regarding the second precept on the prohibition against engaging in trade that invites censure: whereas the preceding rule concerned instigating war and strife, this one concerns the trafficking of people;
furthermore, while the former involved harming living beings so as to cause death, this involves suppressing free persons and reducing them to slavery, which is why it follows immediately after.
The text has two parts: first, a general statement of what is improper.
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally trades in free persons, male or female slaves, or six kinds of domestic animals, or deals in coffins, wooden planks,
and other implements for containing the dead, they should not do so themselves, much less teach others to do so.
The commentary states: Regarding "free persons and slaves," it may be that for one matter a free person is reduced to servitude, or for two matters.
Regarding "livestock," the *Ritual of Zhou* (*Zhouli*) says: oxen, horses, dogs, sheep, pigs, and chickens; in fact, this refers to all types of domestic animals.
As for "trading in coffins and the like," these are the occupations of the *caṇḍālas*, who carry out the burial of the dead.
Although it contains all that remains to be known, within this there are three matters; if these were explained separately, they would constitute three distinct precepts.
Subsequently, both are combined to conclude the prohibition against transgressions.
If one intentionally acts for oneself or instructs another to act, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).

The commentary states: Regarding these matters of purchase, there may be instances of sale; however, as there are no explicit texts [regarding this], one should understand the details of the prohibitions and permissions, as well as the gains and losses, by consulting them thoroughly.
○ Third, regarding the precept against groundless slander: previously, one did not disparage those in lower positions; now, one must not disparage those in higher positions.

Because it is light and does not involve slander, it is placed next. The text has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the definition of the offense for violating the prohibition.
Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the establishment of what should be refrained from.
"If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, slanders others without cause—whether they be virtuous people, good people, Dharma masters, teachers, or monks..."
The King’s Noble Consort said: "One commits the seven inversions and the ten grave offenses.
The commentary states: "An evil mind constitutes the cause for slander; this extends to resentment and jealousy.

To speak of what does not exist as being 'rootless'—that is, to speak of faults where no root exists—is why it constitutes slander. Below this is the category of slandering persons, which consists of six types that are combined into three."

Because these two pairs are combined, they may both be understood in detail; as for the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) and so forth, which are the sins of slander, they are not mentioned separately because the heavy cases serve as examples for the light ones.
This concludes the section on what ought to be practiced according to later regulations.
One should give rise to a mind of filial piety and a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward one’s parents, brothers, and the six classes of relatives.
The commentary states: this text is an abbreviated parallel to the preceding section; otherwise, there would be a contradiction.

A "mind of filial piety" means that when one's parents or superiors have faults, one offers admonition without showing a change in countenance; this constitutes filial piety. Loving-kindness and compassion [are as previously defined].
To feel toward younger siblings and those below them a mind that repents their transgressions and virtues, uproots their suffering karma, and causes them to find peace and happiness hereafter—
this is compassion. If, however, one subsequently violates prohibitions and incurs guilt,
yet instead of reforming further commits acts of rebellion and harm, thereby falling into an undesirable state, this constitutes an offense of light defilement.
The commentary states: To respond with direct accusations of such faults as being unfilial is already a transgression; how much more so to add slander and defilement?
Is this not to go against the natural flow and fall into an undesirable state? It causes one's parents and others to fall into the ranks of the wicked—that is, the realm of unrighteousness.
Except for those who transform through the power of reversal (parāvṛtti), none of these [actions] are permissible.

○ Fourth, regarding the precept against damaging by fire: this follows the sequence of the primary retribution and its secondary environment. The text has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure practice;
second, the definition of the offense for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, citing an event to bring it to awareness;
second, establishing the regulation to effect cessation. Within the first of these, there are two further points: first, citing the cause of the burning.
"If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind...
[The commentary states: "An 'evil mind' applies to both resentment and profit; this subsequently indicates the objects to be burned.
To set forth a great fire to burn mountains, forests, wildernesses, or open lands from the fourth month through the ninth month, or to set fire to another's property."
Regarding houses, dwellings, cities, monasteries, fields, trees, spirits, demons, official property, and all things that have an owner:

the commentary explains this in two parts. First, it clarifies the case of ownerless places; although these lack an owner, they serve as a basis for the consciousness of sentient beings, so if they are set on fire, how could there not be injury?
For this reason, such acts also constitute a violation of the precept against killing. Second, it clarifies the case of things that have an owner.

The *Wutong shuo* (Exposition on the Penetration of Things) states that while there are generally six [types of fire], specifically ten are clarified; these are visible in the text. Later, regulations were established to prohibit them, stating that one must not intentionally burn [fire] in such places.
The commentary explains that in locations without an owner, from the first day of the tenth month until the end of the third month, it is permitted [to light fires] where there is an owner.
Regarding objects, it is improper regardless of the season; "intentionally" means with a malicious mind. If one subsequently violates a prohibition, one incurs an offense.
If one intentionally burns [an object], one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
The commentary states: To harm living beings and damage their possessions is utterly lacking in compassion; upon careful examination, such an act cannot possibly be permitted.

Regarding the fifth precept, "Violating the Dharma through Conversion," which contradicts the fundamental tenets: whereas the preceding [precepts] concerned external harm, this concerns internal harm.

The text has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the imposition of evil consequences for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, citing the circumstances [of the offense].
"If a Buddha's disciple [harms] other Buddha's disciples, non-Buddhists, evil persons, the six types of relatives, or any virtuous spiritual friends.
The commentary states: "The five categories and ten classes may be understood through their expansion and contraction; these are subsequently established as precepts to be practiced."
One should instruct each person individually to receive and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas;

one should teach them to understand the principles and meanings so that they may give rise to the bodhicitta, the ten cittas of departure, the ten cittas of nurturing, and the ten adamantine cittas, explaining to each of them the sequential application of these dharmas.

The commentary states: "In sequence" means that causing one to uphold the teachings, realize the principle, initiate practice, abide in the stages, and proceed toward the goal follows the same order as previously described.

This refers to the successive stages of practice and realization, such as entering, abiding, and emerging. These dharmas pertain universally to both the afflictions to be abandoned and the truths to be realized.

The principle and function apply universally to both the two types of wisdom—the wisdom that abandons and the wisdom that realizes—or alternatively, they refer to the operational modes within the thirty moments of mind.

Thus, the general designation of "the application of the Dharma" (dharmaprayoga) involves two different explanations—*āśraya-prayoktṛ* (the basis and the agent) and *karma-prayoga* (the object and the application)—which, when applied respectively, avoid the faults of overreaching [the superior] or encroaching upon [the inferior], allowing one’s progress and retreat to be measured with propriety. Subsequently, one incurs an offense for violating prohibitions.

If a Bodhisattva, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, arbitrarily teaches the Śrāvaka sūtras and vinayas, or the heterodox treatises of external paths and false views to those of the Two Vehicles, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
The commentary explains: "An evil mind" refers solely to the intention that the teaching might not result in great benefit; "a mind of anger" refers to resentment toward the specific recipient.
If there is a person who instructs another in the Mahāyāna, yet that instructor, out of anger, instead deviously teaches them the Hīnayāna so that they might practice it—
intending for the teacher’s own instruction not to be fulfilled— the words of such a "cross-teaching" appear to have this implication;
or perhaps it is simply that the person being taught, because it contradicts their inclinations, does not reveal the Great Dharma to them crosswise.
The Teacher, being fortunate enough to possess great faculties, bestows the minor Dharma upon them; it is like placing foul food into a precious vessel.

How much more so when dealing with those who are heterodox and perverse—is this not a transgression? If, in truth, there is no evil intent or anger, but rather the realization that they are of small capacity and unfit to receive the Great [Dharma], or if one intends to subdue them, or to master other schools, or to perfect the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), then [the teaching is justified].
Even if one instructs [the student] in this way, there is no offense.
○ Sixth, the precept against borrowing items to seek profit. Previously, the Mahāyāna was not mentioned; here it is mentioned because that [previous section] was presented in reverse order.

The text has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the definition of the offense for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sections. First:
Following the presentation of the conditions for the precepts, the practice of the precepts is now established;

herein begins the first section. O Sons of the Buddha, you should, with a sincere mind, first study the Mahāyāna Vinaya and Sūtras that extensively explain the meanings and flavors [of the teachings].
Once you have seen this, if there are newly initiated Bodhisattvas who come from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li* seeking the Mahāyāna Vinaya and Sūtras, [you should assist them].
The commentary states: Those with a good heart originally desire to benefit themselves and others;

therefore, those who study majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) understand their proper conduct—going and coming, opening and explaining, and so forth—and thus comprehend where they are headed. Otherwise, if one merely displays majestic deportment in vain, what ultimate benefit is there?

This can be understood by observing how later students revere such exemplary conduct. Next follows the section on establishing the precepts, which has two parts. First, it demonstrates ascetic practice (*duṣkaracaryā*)...

To achieve merit, one should, in accordance with the Dharma, explain that all ascetic practices— whether burning the body, the arms, or the fingers, or not burning the body, arms, or fingers to make offerings to the Buddhas—
are not [the path of] a renunciant bodhisattva, even down to [offering to] hungry tigers, wolves, and lions.
All hungry ghosts (*preta*) should offer their own bodies, flesh, hands, feet, and limbs as an offering to him.

The commentary divides this into two parts: first, the supreme offering through which one repays the immense kindness of the Buddha’s peerless virtue, for since one's own body is non-dual [with the Buddha], what greater way is there to repay such great grace than through this offering?
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana (Joyful Vision) is an example of this. Second, even down to... [the lower offerings].

Descending to provide succor with earnest aspiration, he originally resolved upon the Great Mind; forgetting his own body to benefit all beings, if he had encountered this [opportunity] and not been able to save them, what would his vow have served?
Prince Sattva was precisely such a person. Later, he proclaimed the wondrous Dharma to increase wisdom.
Thereafter, he expounded the True Dharma to each one in successive order, causing their minds to open and their intentions to be understood.
The commentary states: The Mahāyāna teachings—its principles, practices, and fruits—constitute the True Dharma; the stages of awakening and cultivation constitute the sequence.

This is as described in the sixth assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Giving Rise to Understanding," following which [the section on] transgressing prohibitions occurs.

Regarding the determination of the offense: if a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and honor, fails to answer when they ought to, or explains the words of the sutras and vinaya in a distorted manner— neither following the proper sequence nor maintaining their integrity—
and thus slanders the Triple Gem, the speaker commits a minor offense (light dust-offense).

The commentary states: Regarding those who act for the sake of gain and offerings, because they invite [others] to seek through hardship and fear that their own gains might be diminished, one should respond or not respond;

"not responding" means either remaining entirely silent or answering truthfully when questioned, while "equivocating, speaking perversely, and so forth" refers to the mutual interchange of precepts and meditative concentration, or applying these principles generally to all lower stages.
This refers to the discrepancy between the beginning and the end; as for those who slander the Triple Gem, the Buddha does not act in such a manner.
If one preaches the Dharma not in this way, or transmits the Saṃgha not in this way, speaking falsely in such a manner, it constitutes slandering the Triple Gem. However,

if it is true and not for the sake of gain, but rather intended to skillfully guide and inspire others according to their meaning and capacities without relying on the literal text, then there is no fault.
○ Seventh: To forcibly seek ordination by relying on official authority; previously, one relied on the Dharma to take profit, which is precisely seeking wealth by relying on official power.
Furthermore, the former was deception, while this is the use of intimidation. The text has four parts; first, the cause of the offense is presented.
"If a Buddha’s disciple, for the sake of food, drink, money, wealth, or gain—namely, for the sake of 'nourishment' (yǎng)—[acts thus].
The commentary explains: "Gain" refers to the provisions of clothing and food; "reputation" refers to the fame of power and influence.
Alternatively, it may mean that having obtained wealth, one gives it away in return to seek a good reputation. Second, the conditions for the offense.
"Associating with kings, princes, ministers, and officials.
The commentary explains: "Kings" refers specifically to those of minor rank; "princes" includes all [ruling] kings; "ministers" encompasses both generals and prime ministers;
and "officials" refers to those who govern prefectures and counties—these three manifest the characteristics of transgression.

Relying on the creation of intimidating displays to beg, strike, drag, and pull others to take money and goods by force, seeking profit in every way—this is called evil seeking, excessive seeking, and inciting others to seek; it is utterly devoid of compassion and devoid of filial piety.

The commentary states: "Relying on one's status and so forth, depending upon superiors, and manifesting their wrath through beating and striking" means that one strikes with a staff to cause pain and beats them to instill fear.
First, one begs [for what is desired], but when it is not obtained, one drags and pulls;

this dragging and pulling to force a superior to take [what is wanted] against the principles of righteousness is the way of all those who seek profit, for they employ every stratagem in their schemes.
Because these things are all sought after, those who seek them wickedly beat and strike others to take them by force;
because those who seek much increase their greed once they have obtained them and remain unsatisfied, this is also "seeking everything.
To teach others to seek means to instruct superiors or officials, to drive others into service, or to instruct other individuals to seek in such a manner; thus, there is affliction below.
Sentient beings lack a compassionate heart, which is a violation of the Buddha’s teachings and a lack of filial piety.

Furthermore, since all sentient beings have been one's own parents, to afflict them is also called unfilial. Moreover, by committing evil deeds oneself, one follows [the path] to be born as an evil person;
this not only fails to save the spirits of the netherworld but also brings calamity upon one's present life—this too is called unfilial. (4) This concludes the section on the commission of offenses.
One commits a minor offense (light defilement).

The commentary states: According to this principle, one also commits the preparatory act (*prayoga*) for the precept against stealing; because it serves as a gateway [to the full offense] and differs in its specific manifestation, it is included here in this text.

Alternatively, if one seizes the goods of a thief to return them to the owner, or disciplines the thief to cause them to plant roots of merit and so forth, it does not result in self-benefit through such conditions.
If one is solely intent on benefiting others and takes a compassionate heart as the foundation, then it may be permitted.

○ Eighth: The Precept Against Acting as a Teacher Without Understanding. The preceding [precept] concerned seeking profit by relying on official authority; this concerns falsely claiming understanding to act as a teacher.
Part One: The Initial Formulation of the Precept to Ensure Practice.

If a disciple of the Buddha studies and recites the precepts, they should daily, during the six periods, uphold the Bodhisattva precepts and understand their meaning—the nature of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
The commentary states:
Diligently recite the text without fail during the six periods; profoundly penetrate its principles so that the two truths (*satyadvaya*) are clearly distinguished.

"Principle" (*li*) refers to the fundamental way of things; "Buddha-nature" (*foxing*) refers to ultimate truth. It is called "the nature of Buddha-nature" (*foxing zhi xing*) in order to distinguish it from other natures.
Furthermore, "principle" refers to the dharmas of upholding and violating [the precepts], while "Buddha-nature" refers to the nature of both original and newly cultivated conduct.
This "nature" is the equal, rational nature; subsequently, one incurs the offense of violating prohibitions.
If a bodhisattva does not understand a single phrase, a single verse, or the causes and conditions of the precepts,
yet falsely claims to understand them, they are deceiving themselves and likewise deceiving others. If, not understanding even a single thing among all dharmas,
they act as a teacher for others and bestow the precepts upon them, they commit a secondary offense (light defilement).

The commentary states: One can discern the differences between the phrasing and the meaning of the verses. Regarding "causes and conditions," this applies to all matters such as the gravity or lightness of transgressions, the observance or violation of precepts, receiving instruction, and the transmission and recitation of the teachings;
in all these cases, causes and conditions are fully present. As for "deceiving oneself and others," both parties fall into error.
As for "not knowing," it refers to one’s own presumption that does not allow others to know one's own lack of understanding. To follow the text literally, it says "one."
If one does not understand each of all phenomena and yet acts as a teacher for others whom one does not know, receiving precepts would indeed be easy; however,
if there is no one to serve as a teacher, then according to what one understands oneself, provided one does not conceal one's shortcomings, there is no fault.
○ Ninth Precept: Slandering and Deceiving the Worthy. Previously, one was inwardly hidden in ignorance; now, one outwardly deceives those of virtue.
Part Two: First, envying the worthy and being jealous of the capable.
If, O Sons of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, you see a precept-keeping bhikṣu holding a fragrant incense burner while practicing the bodhisattva path.

The commentary states: "A malicious mind" refers to either fearing an encroachment upon one's reputation and profit, or harboring resentment from past enmity; any such state that opposes wholesome qualities is termed a malicious mind.
Regarding those who maintain the precepts, they must balance both the light and heavy aspects of discipline. As for those who hold incense burners, they practice the Way through ritual offerings;
yet later, their accumulated evils will result in calamity.
To engage in mutual strife, to slander and deceive others under false pretenses, and to commit every kind of evil—this constitutes a minor offense (laghu-āpatti).

The commentary explains: when neither party has committed a fault, yet each side speaks falsely against the other, causing those of virtuous mind to give rise to resentment and malice, and leading them to mutually oppress and harm one another—it is for this reason that it is so stated. Furthermore, "committing every kind of evil" refers to this person engaging in various [transgressions].
To engage in strife and slander with the intent of causing mutual opposition—there is no evil one does not commit. This is strictly forbidden, except in cases of insanity or mental derangement;
otherwise, it is not permissible. Tenth:
The Precept Against Failing to Rescue Sentient Beings. Previously, [the precept] concerned causing others to abandon what is wholesome; this, however, concerns failing to act when seeing suffering.

Section Two: Saving Sentient Beings. Part One: First, the formulation of the precept to practice; second, the inflicting of punishment for violating the prohibition. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, a general indication;
second, a detailed exposition. This is the first.
"If, O Sons of the Buddha, out of a heart of compassion, you engage in the practice of releasing living beings..."
The commentary states: Compassion is the essence, and the release of living beings is the activity. Activity is practice; practice is conduct; conduct is application.

Regarding the subsequent detailed exposition in two parts: first, the correct contemplation based on principle; second, the arising of practice based on that contemplation. Within the former, there are two sections:

first, contemplating [all beings] as being the same as one's parents; second, contemplating them as being the same as oneself. Within the first of these, there are two further points: first, universally clarifying that all...
Following this, regarding the "unreasonable" [objections] among the two [categories] of the preceding and intermediate [sections], the first addresses the human race:
"All men are my fathers; all women are my mothers; in every birth, there is none from whom I have not received life."
The commentary is divided into two parts: first, the brief presentation; second, the detailed explanation beginning with "I am born again and again.

Alternatively, one might ask: how is it known that all [beings] have parents? Therefore, this is said: through the causal conditions of affection and karma, they become kinsmen and repeatedly undergo countless births;
such is the logical necessity. Subsequently, this is discussed in terms of the six realms of existence (*ṣadgati*).
"All sentient beings of the six realms have been my parents.
The commentary states: "Alternatively, because one's own self has participated in each of the six realms over the course of many kalpas, it must be so.
This concludes the section on what is improper."
To kill and eat [them] is to kill one's own parents.
The commentary asks: "If this is so, why does killing living beings not collectively constitute a heinous crime (*ānantarya-karma*)? It answers:
"Because there is a separation of lifetimes, the perception of them as having the characteristics of one's parents is absent; therefore, one later regards them as being the same as one's own body."
"Because they have killed my former body; all earth and water are my previous bodies, and all fire and wind are my fundamental essence.
The commentary divides this into two parts: first, the brief statement; second, from "all... onwards, the detailed explanation. Alternatively, one might ask: how is this known?

Since this has already been established, it is merely stated here for the sake of the mind’s intention, which says: "The body I have received is likewise the substance of the four great elements of sentient beings;
the bodies thus relinquished are infinite, and it is clear that these are the future bases upon which my observation arises.
This section has two parts: first, a general summary based on what preceded; second, a detailed analysis according to specific matters. This is the first [part].
Therefore, one should constantly practice releasing living beings; this is the dharma of constant abiding through birth after birth, and one teaches others to release living beings.

The commentary explains that, according to the two meanings above, it is fitting that at every place where one undergoes birth, one should constantly practice the rite of releasing living beings as a natural and eternal rule;
thus it is called the "dharma of constant abiding. Not only is it so for oneself, but it also applies to others.

This teaches the practice of the two benefits for oneself and others. The subsequent section distinguishes the text according to specific matters in two parts; first, universally rescuing other lives:
"If one sees people of the world killing animals, one should employ skillful means to rescue and protect them, liberating them from their suffering and hardship;
one should constantly teach and explain the Bodhisattva precepts to save and deliver sentient beings."

The commentary is divided into two parts. First, regarding the specific means of rescuing those in peril: if one does not act in this way, the rescue will not be achieved and may even result in further harm.

Second, regarding the constant teaching and transformation of others as a general means of universal rescue for the remainder: since all beings have been one's parents, they certainly ought to be rescued and delivered;

as this applies horizontally to all people and things and vertically to both the hidden and the manifest, it is appropriate to treat them all universally. Finally, there is the specific provision for the present.
Furthermore,
on the anniversary of the death of one's parents or siblings, one should invite a Dharma Master to lecture on the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra; by dedicating this merit to the deceased,
they shall attain the vision of the Buddhas and be reborn among humans or in the heavens.

The commentary is divided into two parts. First, regarding the filial son’s offering: through this, it is seen that the parents of one’s present life differ from other categories, as their status—whether living or deceased—is knowable;

whereas for other lives, although they are all one’s parents, they are distant and difficult to know. Furthermore, because past lives are vast and numerous, [the teaching] is constantly expounded. For this reason, the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Treasury) states: [The text continues: "By taking only the anniversary of the death (*jichén*) as the occasion for exposition, although other lives are all one's parents, they are remote and difficult to discern. Moreover, since past lives are exceedingly many, [the practice] is performed by constant exposition. Therefore, the *Zangshu* says:"
Within this precept, two matters are fully contained: first, the merit serves as a resource for deceased ancestors so that they may enjoy blessings;
specifically, for those already residing among humans or devas, it causes them to be reborn in a Pure Land, which is why it is said they "shall behold the Buddhas.

If they are in the three miserable realms (*trāya*), they cannot be reborn together in a Pure Land; therefore, it causes them to ascend to the human or heavenly realms. This primarily clarifies the present state while concurrently [addressing the past].
The intent of other similar sūtras is likewise; subsequently, one incurs an offense by violating a prohibition.
If it were not so, one would incur a minor offense (light impurity).
The commentary states: if it is beyond one's power, if there is no teacher to be requested, or if one is personally incapable, yet there is a great benefit [to be gained].
Beyond this, it is not permissible to practice [the precepts] in a partial or inconsistent manner. At the conclusion, the exhortation points toward the extensive [explanation].
Thus, these ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind, as the characteristics of each individual precept are explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Extinction of Sin."
From here below is the third section, clarifying the ten precepts such as "Requiting Enmity," which follows the same format as the preceding sections and consists of ten parts.

○ First is the precept against lacking compassion and requiting enmity; whereas the previous [precept] concerned failing to rescue those who suffer, this one concerns giving rise to resentment toward an enemy.

The Response to the Text, Part Two: First, the initial establishment of the precepts to ensure their practice; second, the subsequent formulation of offenses for violating prohibitions. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, a general indication of what is to be abandoned;
second, a specific enumeration of what is to be abandoned. Now, the first part:
The Buddha said, "O Son of the Buddha, you must not repay anger with anger, nor repay a blow with a blow."

The commentary states: Combining "reprimanding in return for reprimands" with the other two, they together constitute the three karmas. Now, having combined body and mind, the text separately lists those things to be abandoned.
This section has two parts: first, listing the grave offenses, and second, listing the minor ones.
If one kills one's parents, siblings, or other members of the six types of kin, one must not seek retribution; even if a sovereign is killed by another, one likewise must not seek retribution.
To kill in order to provoke further killing does not accord with the Way of Filial Piety.
The commentary states: The first section of these two parts formally establishes the prohibition by citing the cases of close relatives and the most honored to serve as analogies for all others.
The second section demonstrates the underlying reason. Someone might ask: "If one does not repay the enmity of a sovereign or a parent, how can one be called loyal or filial?
It is for this reason that the text says: "Life arises from destiny," meaning that one takes away another's life in order to restore one's own life; hence it is so stated.
Taking life results in enmity being born from enmity; because such resentment does not cease, it is not the way of filial piety, as in the case of King Vairāṭya.
Furthermore, since those enemies were also one's own parents, it is inconsistent with the Buddha’s mind and does not accord with correct principle;
therefore, it is impermissible. Subsequently, the light case is used to illustrate the grave.

If one does not even keep slaves or servants, yet daily commits immeasurable verbal offenses through the three karmas of striking, beating, and insulting them, how much more so for intentionally committing the seven heinous crimes (*ānantarya*)?
The commentary states: "Slaves and servants are lowly beings who belong to oneself; the offenses of striking and insulting them are already many, let alone [offending] an enemy."
If one kills one's own parents, it is identical to the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*). The gravity of the crime of these seven heinous offenses need not be stated further.

Regarding "immeasurable verbal offenses," this refers to cases where people treat their slaves and the like in such a manner; perhaps the character "de" (得) was a scribal error for "di" (違), and thus later violations were codified as offenses.
If an ordained bodhisattva lacks compassion and seeks revenge—even against those as close as the six types of kin—and thus retaliates, they commit a minor offense (*laghu-āpatti*).
The commentary states: "To give rise to the bodhicitta is what constitutes being 'ordained'; this does not depend on outward appearance or robes. Were it otherwise, one would be a lay bodhisattva."
Does Śāriputra not incur an offense? Because the middle [category] subsumes both the beginning and the end, he speaks only of the six types of relatives.
Based on this, it also includes the two grave offenses of killing and malice; the meaning of their allowance or prohibition is as explained in the precept on killing.
○ Second, regarding the person of pride who disparages the Dharma and the precepts: previously, by giving rise to anger toward an object of enmity, they invited great loss;

now, by giving rise to pride toward a person of virtue, they lose great benefit. The text has two parts: first, the establishment of the precept to ensure its practice; second, the definition of the offense for violating the prohibition.

Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the establishment of what should be ceased; second, the establishment of what should be practiced. Within the first of these, there are two further subsections.
Clarifying the causes for the precepts:
O sons of the Buddha, when you have first left the household life and have not yet attained understanding, yet you rely on your own cleverness and intelligence;
or you rely on your noble status and advanced age; or you rely on a prestigious lineage, a high-ranking family, great learning, great merit, or great wealth and abundance of the seven treasures.
"Because of this arrogance, they do not consult or receive the sūtras and vinaya from learned Dharma masters.
The commentary explains that this is divided into three parts: first, the reality that there is nothing understood; second, the two intentions of the one who has left home, namely body and mind;

and third, since the body necessarily entails the mind, if one does not give rise to the Great Mind, one is not a bodhisattva. Thus, the initial statement regarding "leaving home" implies a lack of understanding.
Regarding the second cause, there are ten types of people who rely solely on their noble lineage from below: first, those with keen intelligence, sharp faculties, and acute hearing;
second, those possessing wisdom who are thoroughly conversant with worldly affairs; third, those who were formerly high-ranking officials; fourth, those who are aged and senior;

fifth, those belonging to great clans such as the *kṣatriya* lineages; sixth, those from prestigious families whose ancestors wore robes and necklaces; seventh, those who are highly proficient in the registers of the state (*huángjí*); [and so forth].
Alternatively, there are those of the Hīnayāna who possess the eight great merits, having previously performed great acts of giving;

they are endowed with nine riches, abundant wealth, money and silks, and seventeen treasures such as gold and silver. Because they are ashamed of their inferiority compared to these [superior qualities], they inquire about this set of ten.

Among these ten, one may possess only one or several, and it is not necessary for a single person to be fully endowed with all ten. Hereafter, the conditions for the establishment of the precepts will be explained.
As for this Dharma Master, he may be of low birth, young, from an humble family, poor, or deficient in his faculties, yet he truly possesses virtue and understands all the sūtras and vinayas.

The commentary states that this is divided into two parts: first, regarding his outward appearance, which is unsightly and comprises five types; furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that these characteristics belong to a single individual.

Regarding the preceding text, there are both general and specific [distinctions]. The "specific" refers to those of minor lineage who were objects of the pride of those of major lineage, and so forth.

The "general" should be understood as applying mutually between these two categories; however, in reality, one whose inner virtue is profound is precisely one whose conduct is perfected, for such a person possesses both conduct and understanding.
Thus, by this contrast, the error of pride is clarified. This is what follows from the subsequent regulation.
[This is] an action.
Furthermore, a newly initiated bodhisattva must not examine the lineage of the Dharma teacher.
The commentary states: To briefly cite one instance that may serve as an analogy for all others—consider, for example, when a youth seeks [refuge] from a rākṣasa deity.
The Emperor knelt before the jackal; because his longing for the Dharma was so earnest, he did not regard the faults of its wretched appearance.

This is sufficient to clarify that on the path, how could one openly follow one's own inclinations to the detriment of what is beneficial? Such cases abound in the world—how lamentable, how lamentable!
Later, he violated the prohibitions and incurred guilt.
If one does not come to consult and receive the Dharma Master’s teaching on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one commits a minor offense (*āpatti*).
The commentary explains: regarding the failure to inquire about both truths, the text is abbreviated here.

This excludes cases where one refrains out of self-reliance or contempt for others, or is obstructed by illness or hardship, or knows with certainty that the teacher lacks virtue, or acts to subdue the wicked, or to avoid causing great harm, and so forth.
It may be [permissible] for others, but not for this person.

○ Third, regarding the precept against seeking instruction from those junior to oneself: previously, one did not inquire of those with virtue; here, although there is an inquiry, one does not speak [of it].
Furthermore, previously one was arrogant toward seniors; this [precept] involves slighting juniors—this is the sequence. The text has two parts; first, the enactment of the precept.
Regarding the subsequent transgressions of prohibitions and the formation of offenses, there are two parts: first, a general indication of the time of receiving the precepts;
second, a detailed explanation of the method for receiving the precepts. Now, for the first:
"If, O Sons of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one wishes to receive the Bodhisattva precepts with a sincere mind..."
The commentary states: Regarding "the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and so forth," while the Buddha was still present, there were no such matters as self-vows or receiving the precepts [by oneself].
"With a good mind" means having a sincere aspiration and deep faith; it refers to a mind dedicated solely to the two benefits (self and others).

This "desire with a good mind" distinguishes [the candidate] from one with an evil mind, who is not a fit vessel for receiving the precepts. Following this, the method for receiving the precepts is explained separately in two parts; first:
This section specifically clarifies the subsequent dual conclusion regarding the limits of training. Within this, there are two parts: first, the explanation of self-vowed reception of the precepts;

second, the explanation of receiving them from a teacher. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, a general explanation of the place and ritual; second, a specific clarification of the time and conditions. This is the first [of the two].
Regarding the vow to receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva:
the commentary explains that when the aspiration arises within one’s mind, one establishes a great vow through sincere words and makes a personal commitment expressed orally.

When the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is performed according to the instructions and the signs appear, it is called "attaining the precepts. Subsequently, the text separately clarifies the conditions for the timing [of attainment] in two parts; first, it specifically explains the variations in speed [of attainment].
One should perform repentance before the Buddha for seven days; upon seeing a favorable sign, one may then receive the precepts.
If a favorable sign is not obtained, one should continue for two weeks, three weeks, or even up to a year, until a favorable sign is attained.
Once a favorable sign has been obtained, one receives the Buddha and Bodhisattva precepts before an image of the Buddha.
